enc.title: Choudhuri 1.1: Mass of the Galaxy from the Sun’s orbit
enc.goal: The Sun is about $8$ kpc from the galactic centre and moves on a nearly circular orbit at about $220\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Make a rough estimate of the mass of the Galaxy.

steps.prompt: Which force provides the centripetal acceleration, and which mass counts?
steps.reveal: Gravity of the mass $M$ inside the orbit (for a roughly spherical distribution the outer mass exerts no net force): $\dfrac{v^2}{R}=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}$.
steps.explain: Circular orbit = gravity supplies the centripetal force. For a spherical mass distribution only the mass inside the orbit pulls (shell theorem: the shells outside cancel). So the Sun's orbit "weighs" the Galaxy inside $8$ kpc, exactly like a planet's orbit weighs the Sun.

steps.prompt: Solve for $M$ and put in the numbers.
steps.reveal: $M=\dfrac{v^2R}{G}=\dfrac{(2.2\times10^5)^2\,(8\times3.09\times10^{19})}{6.67\times10^{-11}}\approx 1.8\times10^{41}\ \mathrm{kg}\approx 9\times10^{10}\,M_\odot$.
steps.explain: Multiply $\frac{v^2}{R}=\frac{GM}{R^2}$ by $R^2/G$. Units: convert kpc to m ($8\times3.09\times10^{19}$ m) and km/s to m/s ($2.2\times10^5$). Divide by $M_\odot$ to get solar masses.

steps.reveal: It is the mass inside the solar circle only, about $10^{11}M_\odot$. The flat rotation curve further out (Ch. 6.3) shows that the total mass, dark halo included, is several times larger.
steps.explain: The method only sees mass inside the orbit. Stars and gas further out orbit just as fast (flat rotation curve), so even more mass must be hidden further out: the dark matter halo.

keyPoints: only the mass inside $R$ is measured

enc.title: Choudhuri 1.2: Absolute magnitude and luminosity of a nearby star
enc.goal: A star at a distance of $4$ pc has apparent magnitude $m=2$. Find its absolute magnitude. The Sun has $L_\odot=3.9\times10^{26}$ W and absolute magnitude about $5$: find the luminosity of the star.

steps.prompt: Absolute magnitude: the magnitude the star would have at $10$ pc.
steps.reveal: $M=2-5\log_{10}(0.4)=2+1.99\approx 3.99$. The star is closer than 10 pc, so it would look fainter there ($M>m$).
steps.explain: Distance modulus: flux falls like $1/d^2$, and magnitudes are $-2.5\log_{10}$ of flux, so moving a star from $d$ to $10$ pc changes its magnitude by $5\log_{10}(d/10\,\mathrm{pc})$. $\log_{10}0.4=-0.398$, times $-5$ gives $+1.99$.

steps.prompt: Compare with the Sun using the magnitude scale.
steps.explain: Magnitudes are logarithmic and reversed: 5 magnitudes = factor 100, so 1 magnitude = $100^{1/5}=10^{0.4}\approx2.51$; a smaller magnitude means brighter. The star is one magnitude brighter than the Sun's $M=5$: $10^{0.4}\approx2.5$ times the luminosity.

steps.reveal: $L\approx 2.54\times3.9\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{W}\approx 9.7\times10^{26}$ W, about $2.5L_\odot$.
steps.explain: Multiply the ratio by $L_\odot$. (Absolute magnitudes compare luminosities directly because both stars are imagined at the same 10 pc.)

keyPoints: distance modulus with the right sign

enc.title: Choudhuri 1.3: Resolution of the GMRT
enc.goal: The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope has antennas spread over about $10$ km. Estimate its resolution in arcseconds. How large would an optical telescope have to be for the same resolution in visible light?
given: GMRT works at metre wavelengths (50 MHz to 1.4 GHz, i.e. $\lambda\approx0.2$ to $6$ m)

steps.reveal: An interferometer resolves like a single dish of the size of its longest baseline, $D\approx10^4$ m. Take a typical "metrewave" $\lambda\approx1$ m.
steps.explain: Why the baseline counts. Resolution comes from comparing the phase of a wave at two points: the farther apart, the smaller the angle at which the phase difference changes by a full cycle. An array of antennas therefore resolves like one dish as big as its widest spacing (aperture synthesis).

steps.reveal: $\theta\approx\lambda/D=10^{-4}$ rad $\approx 20.6^{\prime\prime}$. At the 21 cm line it would be $\approx 4.33^{\prime\prime}$.
steps.explain: $\theta\approx\lambda/D$ in radians; to convert, $1\,\mathrm{rad}=206265''$. So $10^{-4}$ rad $\approx20''$.

steps.reveal: $D=\lambda/\theta=5\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}/10^{-4}=5\times10^{-3}$ m: a 5 mm lens. Radio astronomy needs huge apertures because $\lambda$ is $10^6$ times longer (and the atmosphere, not diffraction, limits big optical telescopes to about $1^{\prime\prime}$).
steps.explain: Same formula backwards with $\lambda=500$ nm: a millimetre-sized lens would already match. Radio waves are a million times longer, so radio telescopes must be a million times larger for the same sharpness.

enc.title: Choudhuri 2.3: Saha equation for air-density hydrogen
enc.goal: Hydrogen gas has the density of air at normal conditions, $\rho=1.29\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. With $\chi=13.6$ eV, use the Saha equation (2.29) to calculate the ionization fraction $x$ at different temperatures and plot $x(T)$.
given: Note: Book Fig. and equation numbers refer to Choudhuri; the table was computed with the book constants.

steps.prompt: The density is fixed, the pressure is not. Use the density form of the Saha law.
steps.reveal: With $n_e=n_p=xn$, $n_H=(1-x)n$ and $n=\rho/m_H=7.7\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$: $\dfrac{n_en_p}{n_H}=\dfrac{x^2n}{1-x}=\left(\dfrac{2\pi m_e\kappa_BT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}e^{-\chi/\kappa_BT}$. This is (2.29) with the pressure written as $P=n\kappa_BT$; the pressure form at fixed $P$ would describe a different gas.
steps.explain: Saha is a chemical equilibrium $\mathrm H\rightleftharpoons p+e$: the ratio $n_en_p/n_H$ depends only on $T$ (a Boltzmann factor $e^{-\chi/kT}$ times the phase space available to a free electron). With fixed density $n$ write all three densities through $x$; the left side becomes $\frac{x^2n}{1-x}$.

steps.prompt: Solve for $x$ at a few temperatures (a quadratic in $x$).
steps.explain: Solve the quadratic $nx^2+K(T)x-K(T)=0$ with $K(T)$ the right-hand side: $x=\frac{-K+\sqrt{K^2+4nK}}{2n}$. When $K\ll n$, $x\approx\sqrt{K/n}$, tiny. The exponential $e^{-\chi/kT}$ with $\chi/k=158000$ K makes $K$ rise steeply with $T$.

steps.reveal: $x$ stays tiny up to $\sim10^4$ K and reaches $1/2$ only near $T\approx4\times10^{4}$ K. Ionisation is held back by the high density (recombination is fast); in stellar atmospheres ($n$ much lower) hydrogen ionises near $10^4$ K.
steps.explain: Why so high a temperature: at high density recombination is efficient, so you need a bigger Boltzmann factor to keep atoms ionised. In thin stellar atmospheres the same competition gives ionisation already near $10^4$ K, even though $kT$ is then only about 1 eV, far below 13.6 eV: there are so many free-electron states that entropy wins.

keyPoints: $x(T)$ rises steeply; $x=1/2$ at a few $10^4$ K

enc.title: Choudhuri 2.4: Specific intensity inside a grey atmosphere
enc.goal: Find the specific intensity $I(\tau,\mu>0)$ at an arbitrary optical depth $\tau$ inside a plane-parallel grey atmosphere in the Eddington approximation, with constant flux $F$.

steps.prompt: Substitute the source function into the formal solution.
steps.reveal: $I=\dfrac{3F}{4\pi}\displaystyle\int_\tau^\infty\left(t+\tfrac23\right)e^{-(t-\tau)/\mu}\frac{dt}{\mu}$; put $s=t-\tau$.
steps.explain: Formal solution (2.65): the intensity going up at depth $\tau$ is the emission $S$ of all layers below, each attenuated by $e^{-(t-\tau)/\mu}$ on the slanted way up. Shifting the variable to $s=t-\tau$ (distance below the current depth) makes the integrals standard.

steps.reveal: $\int_0^\infty e^{-s/\mu}ds/\mu=1$ and $\int_0^\infty s\,e^{-s/\mu}ds/\mu=\mu$, so $I(\tau,\mu)=\dfrac{3F}{4\pi}\left(\tau+\mu+\dfrac23\right)$.
steps.explain: $\int_0^\infty e^{-s/\mu}ds=\mu$ and $\int_0^\infty se^{-s/\mu}ds=\mu^2$; dividing by $\mu$ gives 1 and $\mu$. The source function is linear in depth, and a linear function averaged with that exponential weight is simply evaluated one "$\mu$" deeper: $S(\tau+\mu)$.

steps.reveal: At $\tau=0$ this is (2.66) with $q=2/3$. Limb darkening: $I(0,\mu)/I(0,1)=\frac35(\mu+\frac23)$, the centre is brighter than the limb. Deep inside, $I\to S+\frac{3F}{4\pi}\mu$: nearly isotropic with a small outward excess that carries the flux.
steps.explain: Limb darkening: at the disk centre ($\mu=1$) we see down to $\tau\approx1$, at the limb ($\mu\to0$) only the shallow, cooler layers. Deep inside, the $\mu$ term is a small anisotropy, just enough to carry the constant outward flux.

keyPoints: formal solution with the Eddington source function

enc.title: Choudhuri 2.6: Spectrum of a grey atmosphere
enc.goal: How do you calculate the spectrum emerging from a grey atmosphere in the Eddington approximation? (Optionally compute $I_\nu(0,1)$ numerically.) If G is the grey spectrum and R a real one (Fig. 2.11), what can you say about how $\alpha_\nu$ varies with frequency?
given: Note: Fig. 2.11 is only described in our text copy: check the shape of R against G in the book figure.

steps.prompt: Formal solution at the surface, along the normal ($\mu=1$).
steps.reveal: $I_\nu(0,1)=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty B_\nu\big(T(\tau)\big)e^{-\tau}d\tau$ with $T(\tau)$ from (2.69): a weighted sum of Planck curves of the layers down to $\tau\approx1$.
steps.explain: The formal solution at the top with $\mu=1$: add up the Planck emission of each layer, weighted by $e^{-\tau}$ (the fraction that gets out). In a grey atmosphere $\tau$ is the same for all frequencies, and $T(\tau)$ comes from the Eddington solution (2.69).

steps.reveal: For each $\nu$: integrate on a grid in $\tau$ (up to $\tau\approx10$), using $T(\tau)$. The result is close to a Planck curve of $T(\tau\approx2/3)=T_{\rm eff}$, a bit broader because hotter deeper layers add blue light.
steps.explain: Numerics: discretise $\tau$, compute $T$ at each point, evaluate $B_\nu$ and sum with weights $e^{-\tau}\Delta\tau$; contributions beyond $\tau\approx10$ are negligible ($e^{-10}$). The result is dominated by $\tau\approx\frac23$, where $T=T_{\rm eff}$.

Where R lies above G, $\alpha_
u$ is smaller than the mean: we see deeper, hotter layers. Where R lies below G (absorption lines, edges such as the Balmer jump), $\alpha_
u$ is larger: $	au_

steps.explain: The key idea: at each frequency we see down to $\tau_\nu\approx1$. Low opacity: deep and hot, so more light; high opacity: shallow and cool, so less light (absorption lines). Comparing a real spectrum with the grey one therefore tells you where $\alpha_\nu$ is above or below average.

enc.title: Choudhuri 2.7: Thomson scattering in an ionized "atmosphere"
enc.goal: Fully ionized hydrogen has the density of the Earth’s atmosphere. Using Thomson scattering by free electrons, find the path length after which a light beam is reduced to half its intensity. (Why did matter-radiation decoupling only happen after recombination, §11.7?)

steps.reveal: One electron per proton: $n_e=\rho/m_H=1.29/1.67\times10^{-27}=7.7\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$.
steps.explain: Fully ionised hydrogen: one free electron per proton, and the mass is almost all protons, so $n_e=\rho/m_H$.

steps.reveal: $e^{-n_e\sigma_Ts}=\frac12\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{\ln2}{n_e\sigma_T}=13.5$ m.
steps.explain: Attenuation $e^{-n_e\sigma_Ts}$: $n_e\sigma_T$ is the inverse mean free path. Set the factor to $\frac12$, take the logarithm: $s=\ln2\cdot$ mean free path.

steps.reveal: A fully ionized gas of air density is opaque after a few tens of metres. Before recombination the Universe was such a fog: photons scattered constantly. Only when the electrons were bound into atoms ($z\approx1100$) did the mean free path become larger than the horizon, and the CMB photons travel freely.
steps.explain: Free electrons scatter light very efficiently; bound electrons in neutral hydrogen hardly scatter visible light. So the early Universe was opaque until the electrons recombined into atoms, and then suddenly transparent: that moment is the CMB we see.

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.1: Thermal versus gravitational energy of the Sun
enc.goal: Estimate the total thermal energy of the Sun from the fact that its internal temperature is of order $10^7$ K. Show that it is of the same order as the rough estimate of the gravitational potential energy.

steps.reveal: Ionized gas, $\mu\approx0.6$: $N=M_\odot/(0.6m_H)\approx2\times10^{57}$.
steps.explain: Mean molecular weight $\mu$: the average mass per free particle in units of $m_H$. Ionised gas has electrons too, so many particles per unit mass: for mostly hydrogen, $\mu\approx0.6$. $N=M/(\mu m_H)$.

steps.reveal: $E_{\rm th}\approx\frac32N\kappa_B(10^7\ \mathrm K)\approx4.1\times10^{41}$ J.
steps.explain: Each particle has $\frac32\kappa_BT$ of kinetic energy (equipartition, three directions). Multiply by $N$.

steps.reveal: $|E_G|\approx GM_\odot^2/R_\odot=3.8\times10^{41}$ J: the same order. This is the virial theorem (§3.2.2): $2E_{\rm th}+E_G=0$, i.e. a self-gravitating gas ball in equilibrium must have $\kappa_BT\sim GMm_H/R$.
steps.explain: Why they must match: gravity tries to compress the star, pressure (thermal motion) resists. In equilibrium the virial theorem $2E_{\rm th}+E_G=0$ fixes the internal temperature from mass and radius alone, which is how we know the Sun's centre is $\sim10^7$ K without seeing it.

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.2: Kelvin–Helmholtz contraction rate
enc.goal: If the Sun produced its energy by slow contraction (Helmholtz and Kelvin), by how much would its radius have to decrease every year to supply the observed luminosity?
given: virial theorem: half of the released gravitational energy is radiated

steps.reveal: $L=\frac12\dfrac{d|E_G|}{dt}=\frac12\dfrac{GM^2}{R^2}\left|\dfrac{dR}{dt}\right|$ (the other half heats the star).
steps.explain: Virial bookkeeping: when a star contracts, gravity releases $\Delta|E_G|$; by $2E_{\rm th}=-E_G$ half of it goes into heating the gas and only half can be radiated. Differentiate $|E_G|=GM^2/R$ in time: $\frac{d}{dt}\frac1R=-\frac{\dot R}{R^2}$.

steps.reveal: $\left|\dfrac{dR}{dt}\right|=\dfrac{2LR^2}{GM^2}=1.4\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx44.5$ m per year (with $E_G=-\frac35GM^2/R$ for a uniform sphere: $\approx74.2$ m/yr).
steps.explain: Solve for $|\dot R|$ and convert: one year is $3.15\times10^7$ s. The prefactor ($1$ or $\frac35$ for a uniform sphere) changes the number but not the order.

steps.prompt: Is that observable, and why is the hypothesis wrong?
steps.reveal: Tens of metres per year is far below what we can measure. The objection is the time scale: $\tau_{KH}\approx|E_G|/2L\approx10^7$ yr, far shorter than the geological age of the Earth.
steps.explain: The real argument is the time scale: the total energy available divided by the luminosity, $\sim10^7$ yr. Geology and fossils need billions of years, so contraction cannot be the Sun's power source: nuclear fusion is.

keyPoints: Kelvin–Helmholtz time $\sim10^7$ yr is too short

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.3: Radiation versus gas pressure in the solar centre
enc.goal: Show that the radiation pressure at the centre of the Sun is negligible compared to the gas pressure, by estimating their ratio.

steps.reveal: $P_{\rm rad}=\frac13a_BT_c^4\approx1.5\times10^{13}$ Pa.
steps.explain: Radiation pressure of blackbody radiation is a third of its energy density, $\frac13a_BT^4$. Use $a_B=7.56\times10^{-16}$ SI and $T^4$ at the centre.

steps.reveal: $P_{\rm gas}=\dfrac{\rho_c\kappa_BT_c}{\mu m_H}\approx3.1\times10^{16}$ Pa.
steps.explain: Ideal gas: $P=nkT$ with $n=\rho/(\mu m_H)$ particles per volume.

steps.reveal: $P_{\rm rad}/P_{\rm gas}\approx4.8\times10^{-4}$. The ratio $\propto T^3/\rho$; for stars on the main sequence it grows with mass (Exercise 5.5), so radiation pressure matters only for massive stars.
steps.explain: Ratio $\propto T^4/(\rho T)=T^3/\rho$: hot, thin matter is radiation dominated. In more massive stars the centre is hotter and less dense, so radiation pressure becomes important (and eventually limits the mass, Ex. 3.5).

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.4: Structure of the solar convection zone
enc.goal: The Sun has a convection zone from $0.7R_\odot$ to the surface. Find how $\rho$, $P$ and $T$ vary in it, assuming (i) (3.22) holds exactly and (ii) the zone contains so little mass that $g=GM_\odot/r^2$.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{d\ln T}{d\ln P}=1-\dfrac1\gamma=\dfrac25$: $P\propto T^{5/2}$ and with the ideal gas $\rho\propto T^{3/2}$ (an adiabat, polytrope $n=3/2$).
steps.explain: (3.22) is the adiabatic temperature gradient: a convection zone is so well mixed that it follows an adiabat. $\frac{dT}{T}=\frac25\frac{dP}{P}$ integrates to $T\propto P^{2/5}$, i.e. $P\propto T^{5/2}$; with $P\propto\rho T$, $\rho\propto T^{3/2}$.

steps.reveal: Insert hydrostatic equilibrium: $\dfrac{dT}{dr}=-\dfrac25\dfrac{T}{P}\dfrac{GM\rho}{r^2}=-\dfrac25\dfrac{GM\mu m_H}{\kappa_Br^2}$: a constant times $1/r^2$.
steps.explain: Insert hydrostatic equilibrium for $dP/dr$ and the ideal gas for $\rho/P$: $\frac{T\rho}{P}=\frac{\mu m_H}{\kappa_B}$, so $T$, $P$ and $\rho$ all drop out and the gradient depends only on gravity.

steps.reveal: $T(r)=\dfrac25\dfrac{GM\mu m_H}{\kappa_B}\left(\dfrac1r-\dfrac1R\right)$, then $\rho=\rho_b\,(T/T_b)^{3/2}$, $P=P_b\,(T/T_b)^{5/2}$.
steps.explain: $\frac{dT}{dr}\propto-\frac1{r^2}$ integrates to $\frac1r$ plus a constant; choose the constant so that $T\approx0$ at the surface (the surface is very cool compared with the interior). Then the adiabat relations give $\rho$ and $P$.

steps.reveal: $T_b=\frac25\times1.4\times10^{7}\ \mathrm K\times(1/0.7-1)\approx2.4\times10^{6}$ K, close to the $2\times10^6$ K of solar models.
steps.explain: Put numbers in: $\frac{GM_\odot\mu m_H}{\kappa_BR_\odot}\approx1.4\times10^7$ K for $\mu=0.6$, times $\frac25$ and $(\frac1{0.7}-1)=0.43$. A simple model already gets the base temperature of the convection zone right.

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.5: Eddington limit and maximum stellar mass
enc.goal: In very hot stars the opacity is Thomson scattering. Show that $L/M$ must be below a critical value and find it; compare with $L_\odot/M_\odot$. Use (3.45) to estimate the maximum mass for which the outer layers are not blown off.

steps.prompt: Balance radiation force and gravity on a gas element.
steps.reveal: Radiative force per unit mass $\chi F/c=\chi L/(4\pi r^2c)$ must be below $GM/r^2$: $\dfrac LM<\dfrac{4\pi cG}{\chi}$. $R$ cancels.
steps.explain: Radiation pushes too: photons carry momentum $E/c$. A gas element with opacity $\chi$ (cross-section per mass) absorbs or scatters a fraction of the flux $F=L/4\pi r^2$ and receives a force $\chi F/c$ per unit mass. Gravity per unit mass is $GM/r^2$. Both fall like $1/r^2$, so the comparison does not depend on $r$.

steps.reveal: $\chi=\sigma_T/m_H=0.0398\ \mathrm{m^2kg^{-1}}$, so $(L/M)_{\max}=6.31\ \mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$; the Sun has $L_\odot/M_\odot=1.9\times10^{-4}$, about $3.3\times10^{4}$ times less.
steps.explain: $\chi=\sigma_T/m_H$: one electron per proton mass. Then $\frac{4\pi cG}{\chi}$ in W/kg; compare with the Sun's $L/M$.

steps.reveal: $\lambda=L_\odot/M_\odot^3$, so $\left(\dfrac{M_{\max}}{M_\odot}\right)^2=\dfrac{(L/M)_{\max}}{L_\odot/M_\odot}\Rightarrow M_{\max}\approx181M_\odot$. Real upper masses are $\sim100M_\odot$: the order is right.
steps.explain: With the mass–luminosity law $L\propto M^3$, $L/M\propto M^2$ grows with mass, so above some mass a star would exceed the Eddington limit and blow its outer layers away. Scale from the Sun: $(M_{\max}/M_\odot)^2$ = ratio of the two $L/M$.

keyPoints: radiative force $\chi L/4\pi r^2c$ versus gravity

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.6: Distance of the globular cluster M3
enc.goal: From Figures 3.5 and 3.8, estimate the distance of the globular cluster M3.
given: a feature of known absolute magnitude in the cluster’s HR diagram
Note: The magnitudes are typical literature values for M3; check them against Figs. 3.5 and 3.8 of the book.

steps.reveal: Fig. 3.8 is the colour–magnitude diagram of M3 in apparent magnitude. Pick a feature whose absolute magnitude you know from Fig. 3.5 (the HR diagram of nearby stars): the horizontal branch ($M_V\approx+0.6$) or the main sequence at the same colour (main-sequence fitting).
steps.explain: Standard candle principle: a feature of the HR diagram with known absolute magnitude, found in the cluster at some apparent magnitude, gives the distance modulus $m-M$ for the whole cluster (all stars at the same distance).

steps.reveal: The horizontal branch of M3 lies at $V\approx15.6$: $m-M\approx15.0$, $d=10^{(m-M+5)/5}$ pc $\approx10^{4}$ pc, i.e. about $10$ kpc.
Reading the figures ($\pm0.3$ mag gives $\pm15\%$ in $d$), metallicity differences between cluster and field stars, and interstellar extinction (small for M3, high galactic latitude).
steps.explain: Magnitudes are logarithmic: an error $\delta m$ gives a relative distance error $\approx0.46\,\delta m$. Dust dims stars (making them look farther), and metal-poor stars have a slightly different main sequence.

keyPoints: shift between apparent and absolute sequence = distance modulus

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.7: Peak wavelengths of a $9M_\odot$ and a $0.25M_\odot$ star
enc.goal: Make a very rough estimate of the wavelengths at which a star of $9M_\odot$ and a star of $0.25M_\odot$ emit maximum radiation.
given: main-sequence $T_{\rm eff}$ from the HR diagram (Fig. 3.5) or scaling laws

steps.reveal: From the HR diagram: a $9M_\odot$ star is an early B star, $T_{\rm eff}\approx2.2\times10^{4}$ K; a $0.25M_\odot$ star is an M dwarf, $T_{\rm eff}\approx3.4e+03$ K.
steps.explain: On the main sequence mass decides everything, so read $T_{\rm eff}$ off the HR diagram at the corresponding spectral type.

steps.reveal: $\lambda_{\max}\approx1.3\times10^{-7}$ m (ultraviolet) and $\approx8.5\times10^{-7}$ m (near infrared).
steps.explain: Wien: $\lambda_{\max}=2.9\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,K}/T$. Hot stars peak in the UV (blue-white), cool dwarfs in the infrared (red).

steps.prompt: Why a pure scaling estimate is poor here.
steps.reveal: $L\propto M^3$ with $R\propto M$ gives $T\propto M^{1/4}$, i.e. only $10^{4}$ K for $9M_\odot$: the radius grows more slowly than $M$ and $L$ faster than $M^3$ for massive stars. Reading the HR diagram is the better rough estimate.
steps.explain: $L=4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$, so $T\propto(L/R^2)^{1/4}$. Crude power laws for $L(M)$ and $R(M)$ give poor $T$ at the extremes; the observed HR diagram is more reliable.

keyPoints: $T_{\rm eff}$ from mass via the main sequence
UV for the massive star, near IR for the M dwarf

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.1: Gamow factor from WKB
enc.goal: Nuclei of charges $Z_1e$, $Z_2e$ approach with relative energy $E$; classically they cannot come closer than $r_1$, $E=\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r_1}$. With WKB show $P\propto\exp\left[-2\displaystyle\int_{r_0}^{r_1}\sqrt{\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}\left(\frac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}-E\right)}dr\right]$ ($m$ reduced mass, $r_0$ nuclear radius). Evaluate the integral with $r=r_1\cos^2\theta$ for $r_1\gg r_0$ and obtain (4.7).

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}-E=E\left(\dfrac{r_1}{r}-1\right)$, so the exponent is $-2\sqrt{\dfrac{2mE}{\hbar^2}}\displaystyle\int_{r_0}^{r_1}\sqrt{\frac{r_1}{r}-1}\,dr$.
steps.explain: Tunnelling through the Coulomb barrier. WKB: inside a forbidden region the wave decays with local rate $\kappa(r)$, and the probability to get through is $e^{-2\int\kappa\,dr}$. The forbidden region runs from the nuclear surface $r_0$ to the classical turning point $r_1$, defined by $V(r_1)=E$. Writing $V=E\,r_1/r$ makes the integrand $\sqrt{r_1/r-1}$.

steps.reveal: $dr=-2r_1\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{r_1/r-1}=\tan\theta$: $\displaystyle\int=2r_1\int_0^{\theta_0}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=r_1\left[\theta_0-\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0\right]$, with $\cos^2\theta_0=r_0/r_1$.
steps.explain: Why $r=r_1\cos^2\theta$: it removes the square root, since $\frac{r_1}{r}-1=\frac1{\cos^2\theta}-1=\tan^2\theta$. With $dr=-2r_1\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta$ the integrand becomes $\tan\theta\cdot2r_1\cos\theta\sin\theta=2r_1\sin^2\theta$, and $\int\sin^2=\frac12(\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta)$.

steps.reveal: $\theta_0\to\pi/2$: the integral $\to\pi r_1/2$ (correction $-2\sqrt{r_0r_1}$, the small "nuclear radius" term).
steps.explain: $r_0\ll r_1$: the lower limit $r=r_0$ means $\cos\theta_0\approx0$, i.e. $\theta_0\to\pi/2$, and $\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0\to0$. The integral is $\frac\pi2r_1$: the barrier is essentially the whole Coulomb tail.

steps.reveal: Exponent $=-2\sqrt{\dfrac{2mE}{\hbar^2}}\dfrac{\pi}{2}\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0E}=-\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\epsilon_0\hbar}\sqrt{\dfrac{2m}{E}}=-\dfrac{1}{2\epsilon_0\hbar}\left(\dfrac m2\right)^{1/2}\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{\sqrt E}$, which is (4.7). Equivalently $P\propto e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$, $E_G=2mc^2(\pi\alpha Z_1Z_2)^2$.
steps.explain: Insert $r_1=\frac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0E}$: the $E$'s combine to $1/\sqrt E$. The probability rises steeply with energy, which is why only the fastest nuclei fuse.

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.2: The pp-chain exponent
enc.goal: For two protons, show that the argument of the exponential in the energy generation rate (4.19) becomes the one in (4.25), $-33.8\,(10^6/T)^{1/3}$.

steps.prompt: Where does the 3 and the cube root come from?
steps.reveal: Maximising $e^{-E/\kappa_BT-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$ (Gamow peak) gives $E_0=(E_G(\kappa_BT)^2/4)^{1/3}$ and exponent $-3(E_G/4\kappa_BT)^{1/3}$; $E_G/4=e^4mZ_1^2Z_2^2/(32\epsilon_0^2\hbar^2)$.
steps.explain: Gamow peak: the rate is (number of nuclei with energy $E$) × (tunnelling probability): $e^{-E/kT}$ falls, $e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$ rises. Their product has a sharp maximum. Set the derivative of the exponent to zero, find $E_0$, and insert it back: the exponent at the peak is $-3(E_G/4kT)^{1/3}$.

steps.prompt: Evaluate the temperature scale for two protons.
steps.reveal: $T_G=\dfrac{e^4(m_p/2)}{32\epsilon_0^2\hbar^2\kappa_B}=1.4\times10^{9}$ K.
steps.explain: For two protons $Z_1=Z_2=1$ and the reduced mass is $m_p/2$. Collect all constants into a temperature $T_G$; its size ($10^9$ K) shows how much the Coulomb barrier suppresses fusion at solar temperatures ($10^7$ K).

steps.reveal: $3\left(\dfrac{T_G}{T}\right)^{1/3}=3\left(\dfrac{T_G}{10^6\ \mathrm K}\right)^{1/3}\left(\dfrac{10^6}{T}\right)^{1/3}=33.7\left(\dfrac{10^6}{T}\right)^{1/3}$, i.e. the 33.8 of (4.25).
steps.explain: Writing $T$ in units of $10^6$ K just pulls the number $3(T_G/10^6\,\mathrm K)^{1/3}=33.8$ out in front.

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.3: Energy generation at the centre of the Sun
enc.goal: The solar centre has $T=1.56\times10^7$ K, $\rho=1.48\times10^5\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $X_H=0.64$, $X_{He}=0.34$, $X_{CNO}=0.015$. Estimate the energy generated per unit volume by the pp chain and the CNO cycle.

steps.explain: Compute the temperature factors once: $(10^6/T)^{1/3}$ and its square. The exponentials are where everything happens: the CNO exponent is 4.5 times bigger (carbon and nitrogen have charge 6–7, a much higher barrier).

steps.reveal: $\varepsilon_{pp}\approx3.1\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$, $\varepsilon_{CNO}\approx6.7\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$.
steps.explain: Insert into the two rate formulas. The CNO prefactor is enormous ($10^{20}$) because once nuclei get through, the reaction is fast; the barrier factor kills most of it at solar temperatures.

steps.reveal: $\approx460\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ (pp) and $\approx99\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ (CNO): the pp chain dominates in the Sun. Only a few hundred watts per cubic metre, less than a compost heap; the Sun is bright because it is huge.
steps.explain: Rates are per kilogram; multiply by the density to get per cubic metre. The tiny power density shows the Sun is not a violent reactor; it is just very large and very well insulated.

steps.reveal: $d\ln\varepsilon/d\ln T=-\frac23+\frac{33.8}{3}(10^6/T)^{1/3}\approx4$ for pp and $\approx20$ for CNO: CNO wins in hotter (more massive) stars.
steps.explain: Sensitivity = logarithmic derivative of $\varepsilon$ with respect to $T$. Differentiating $e^{-a(10^6/T)^{1/3}}$ gives $\frac a3(10^6/T)^{1/3}$. A larger barrier means a steeper temperature dependence: CNO $\propto T^{20}$ wins as soon as the core is a bit hotter.

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.4: Sound crossing time of the Sun
enc.goal: Make a very rough estimate of the time an acoustic wave travelling radially inward would take to go from one end of the Sun to the other.

steps.reveal: Centre ($1.6\times10^7$ K): $c_s\approx5.9\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; a typical interior temperature $5\times10^6$ K: $c_s\approx3.3\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; near the surface only $\sim10\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
steps.explain: Sound speed in an ideal gas is like the thermal speed: $c_s=\sqrt{\gamma kT/\mu m_H}$. Inside the Sun $T$ ranges from $10^7$ K to a few thousand, so pick representative values.

steps.reveal: $t\approx2R_\odot/\langle c_s\rangle\approx4.18e+03$ s, about an hour.
steps.explain: Distance over speed. Using a mean sound speed of a few hundred km/s across $2R_\odot=1.4\times10^9$ m gives about an hour.

steps.reveal: Acoustic modes of the Sun (5-minute oscillations) have periods much shorter than this crossing time; their frequencies probe $c_s(r)$ and thus $T(r)$: helioseismology (§4.4).
steps.explain: Sound waves trapped in the Sun ring at well-defined frequencies; their frequencies depend on $c_s(r)$ along their path. Measuring thousands of such modes maps the interior (helioseismology).

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.5: Mass lost in the solar wind
enc.goal: Near the Earth the solar wind has $v\approx400\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and about $10$ protons per $\mathrm{cm^3}$. If it always had these values during $4.5\times10^9$ yr, what fraction of its mass has the Sun lost?
given: $\dot M=4\pi r^2nm_pv$ through a sphere of radius 1 AU

steps.reveal: $\dot M=4\pi(1.5\times10^{11})^2\times10^7\times1.67\times10^{-27}\times4\times10^5\approx1.9\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$.
steps.explain: Mass flux through a sphere: density × speed × area. Density = proton number density × proton mass ($10$ per cm$^3$ = $10^7$ per m$^3$), area $4\pi(1\,\mathrm{AU})^2$. In a steady wind the same flux passes every sphere, so measuring at the Earth suffices.

steps.reveal: $\Delta M=\dot M\times4.5\times10^9\ \mathrm{yr}\approx2.7\times10^{26}$ kg, a fraction $1.3\times10^{-4}$ of $M_\odot$.
steps.explain: Multiply by the age in seconds ($4.5\times10^9\times3.15\times10^7$ s) and divide by $M_\odot$.

steps.reveal: $L_\odot/c^2\approx4\times10^9\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$: the Sun loses about twice as much mass to radiation as to the wind, both negligible for its evolution.
steps.explain: Radiation also carries mass: $\dot M=L/c^2$ (Einstein). Both are tiny fractions of the Sun's mass over its whole life.

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.6: Neutrino mass from SN 1987A
enc.goal: Neutrinos from SN 1987A travelled $55$ kpc and had energies of $6$–$39$ MeV. If the $12$ s spread in arrival times came from different speeds, show that the neutrino mass cannot be much more than about $20$ eV.

steps.reveal: $\Delta t(E)=\dfrac dc\left(\dfrac cv-1\right)\approx\dfrac dc\dfrac{m^2c^4}{2E^2}$.
steps.explain: A massive particle is slower than light; for $E\gg mc^2$ expand $v/c$: $1-v/c\approx\frac{m^2c^4}{2E^2}$. Travel time $d/v$ exceeds $d/c$ by $\frac dc(\frac cv-1)\approx\frac dc\frac{m^2c^4}{2E^2}$: low-energy neutrinos lag more.

steps.prompt: Difference between the slowest and fastest neutrinos.
steps.reveal: $\Delta t_{6}-\Delta t_{39}=\dfrac dc\dfrac{m^2c^4}{2}\left(\dfrac1{E_1^2}-\dfrac1{E_2^2}\right)\le12$ s, with $d/c=5.7\times10^{12}$ s.
steps.explain: The most delayed (6 MeV) minus the least delayed (39 MeV). If all neutrinos left together, this difference must fit inside the observed 12 s spread.

steps.reveal: $mc^2\le\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times12}{(d/c)(1/36-1/1521)\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}}}}\approx12.5$ eV. The emission itself lasts seconds, so the bound is "not much more than" $\sim10$–$20$ eV.
steps.explain: Solve for $mc^2$, keeping energies in MeV and converting to eV at the end. Because the burst itself lasts seconds, the bound is a rough upper limit, of order 10–20 eV.

keyPoints: delay $\propto E^{-2}$, use the two extreme energies

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.1: Kinetic-theory pressure (5.1)
enc.goal: Derive $P=\frac13\displaystyle\int vp\,f(p)\,4\pi p^2dp$ (5.1) by counting the particles that hit a unit area of the wall per unit time and the momentum they transfer in elastic collisions. Then find $f(p)$ for a Maxwellian (2.27) and show $P=n\kappa_BT$.
given: $4\pi f(p)p^2dp$ = number of particles per volume with momentum in $[p,p+dp]$, isotropic

steps.prompt: Particles with momentum $p$ moving at angle $\theta$ to the wall normal: how many hit unit area per unit time?
steps.reveal: The fraction moving into $d\theta$ is $\frac12\sin\theta\,d\theta$; their flux onto the wall is $v\cos\theta$ times their density: $4\pi f p^2dp\cdot v\cos\theta\cdot\frac12\sin\theta\,d\theta$.
steps.explain: Pressure = momentum delivered to a wall per area per time. Count the particles that hit: those moving towards the wall at angle $\theta$ arrive at the rate (density) × (normal speed $v\cos\theta$). Isotropy means the directions are spread evenly over the sphere: the fraction in $d\theta$ is the area of that ring of the unit sphere over $4\pi$, i.e. $\frac12\sin\theta\,d\theta$.

steps.reveal: Elastic reflection reverses the normal component: $2p\cos\theta$.
steps.explain: An elastic bounce flips the normal component of the momentum, $p\cos\theta\to-p\cos\theta$: the wall receives $2p\cos\theta$.

steps.reveal: $P=\displaystyle\int vp\,f\,4\pi p^2dp\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta=\frac13\int vp\,f\,4\pi p^2dp$ (5.1). It holds for any $v(p)$, also relativistic.
steps.explain: Multiply rate × momentum per hit and integrate over the incoming hemisphere: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta=\frac13$; together with the factors $\frac12$ and $2$ this is the $\frac13$ of (5.1). No assumption about $v(p)$ was used, so it holds for photons and relativistic electrons too.

steps.reveal: $f(p)=n(2\pi m\kappa_BT)^{-3/2}e^{-p^2/2m\kappa_BT}$, $v=p/m$: $P=\dfrac{1}{3m}\displaystyle\int p^2f\,4\pi p^2dp=\dfrac{n\langle p^2\rangle}{3m}=\dfrac{n\cdot3m\kappa_BT}{3m}=n\kappa_BT$.
steps.explain: For a Maxwellian $v=p/m$, so $vp=p^2/m$ and the integral is $n\langle p^2\rangle/3m$. Equipartition $\langle p^2\rangle/2m=\frac32kT$ gives $P=nkT$: the ideal gas law from counting collisions.

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.2: Exact pressure of a degenerate electron gas
enc.goal: Evaluate (5.5), $P=\dfrac{8\pi}{3h^3}\displaystyle\int_0^{p_F}\dfrac{p^4c^2\,dp}{\sqrt{p^2c^2+m_e^2c^4}}$, with $p=m_ec\sinh\theta$ and show $P=\dfrac{\pi m_e^4c^5}{3h^3}f(x)$, $f(x)=x(2x^2-3)\sqrt{x^2+1}+3\sinh^{-1}x$, $x=p_F/m_ec$. Plot $\log P$ against $\log\rho$ and mark the regions of the limits (5.9) and (5.11).

steps.reveal: $dp=m_ec\cosh\theta\,d\theta$, $\sqrt{p^2c^2+m_e^2c^4}=m_ec^2\cosh\theta$, so the integrand becomes $m_e^4c^5\sinh^4\theta\,d\theta$ and $P=\dfrac{8\pi m_e^4c^5}{3h^3}\displaystyle\int_0^{\theta_F}\sinh^4\theta\,d\theta$.
steps.explain: Why $\sinh$: the relativistic energy $\sqrt{p^2c^2+m^2c^4}$ becomes $mc^2\cosh\theta$ (because $\cosh^2-\sinh^2=1$), removing the square root, and $dp$ brings another $\cosh$, which cancels it. What is left is a power of $\sinh$.

steps.reveal: $\sinh^4\theta=\frac18(\cosh4\theta-4\cosh2\theta+3)$, so $\int_0^{\theta_F}=\frac{\sinh4\theta_F}{32}-\frac{\sinh2\theta_F}{4}+\frac{3\theta_F}{8}$. With $x=\sinh\theta_F$: $\sinh2\theta=2x\sqrt{1+x^2}$, $\sinh4\theta=4x\sqrt{1+x^2}(1+2x^2)$, which gives $\frac18f(x)$. Hence $P=\dfrac{\pi m_e^4c^5}{3h^3}f(x)$.
steps.explain: Reduce powers to multiple angles (like $\sin^2=\frac12(1-\cos2x)$): $\sinh^4\theta=\frac18(\cosh4\theta-4\cosh2\theta+3)$, then integrate term by term and express $\sinh2\theta$, $\sinh4\theta$ through $x=\sinh\theta_F$ with double-angle formulas.

steps.reveal: $x\ll1$: $f\approx\frac85x^5$, $P\propto p_F^5\propto\rho^{5/3}$ (5.9). $x\gg1$: $f\approx2x^4$, $P\propto\rho^{4/3}$ (5.11).
steps.explain: Limits: $x=p_F/m_ec$ small means non-relativistic electrons, large means ultra-relativistic. Expanding $f$ gives $x^5$ or $x^4$; with $p_F\propto n_e^{1/3}\propto\rho^{1/3}$ that is $\rho^{5/3}$ or $\rho^{4/3}$. The softer $\frac43$ law is what makes white dwarfs above a certain mass unstable.

steps.reveal: $x=1$ when $n_e=\frac{8\pi}{3}(m_ec/h)^3=5.9\times10^{35}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, i.e. $\rho\approx2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ for $\mu_e=2$. On the $\log P$–$\log\rho$ plot the slope bends from $5/3$ to $4/3$ around there.
steps.explain: Electrons become relativistic when $p_F\approx m_ec$, i.e. $x=1$; convert to $n_e$ with the given formula and to $\rho$ with two nucleons per electron ($\mu_e=2$).

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.3: The polytropic constants $K_1$, $K_2$ and Fig. 5.1
enc.goal: Carry out all the algebra and numbers to obtain (5.9)–(5.12). Then produce Fig. 5.1 (the $T$–$\rho$ plane divided into regions where the ideal gas, non-relativistic and relativistic degenerate equations of state hold) and justify the procedure.

steps.explain: Insert $p_F$ in terms of $n_e$, and $n_e=\rho/(\mu_em_H)$, into the non-relativistic pressure: all constants together form $K_1$ in $P=K_1\rho^{5/3}$. The $\mu_e^{-5/3}$ shows that pressure depends on electrons per mass.
Same with the relativistic formula ($p_F^4$, hence $\rho^{4/3}$). Note $K_2$ contains $c$ but not $m_e$: ultra-relativistic electrons do not care about their mass.

steps.prompt: Boundaries in the $T$–$\rho$ plane: set the competing pressures equal.
steps.reveal: Ideal gas = non-rel. degenerate: $T=\dfrac{\mu m_HK_1}{\kappa_B}\rho^{2/3}\approx228\,\rho^{2/3}$ K. Non-rel. = rel.: $\rho=(K_2/K_1)^3\approx3.8\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Ideal = rel. degenerate: $T\approx3.6\times10^{5}\,\rho^{1/3}$ K. Radiation = gas: $T=\left(\dfrac{3\kappa_B\rho}{a_B\mu m_H}\right)^{1/3}\approx3.8\times10^{6}\,\rho^{1/3}$ K ($\mu=0.6$, $\mu_e=2$, SI).
steps.explain: Each boundary is where two pressure formulas give the same value: e.g. ideal gas $\frac{\rho kT}{\mu m_H}=K_1\rho^{5/3}$ gives $T\propto\rho^{2/3}$. Plotting these lines in the $\log T$–$\log\rho$ plane divides it into regions.

steps.prompt: Why is this the right procedure?
steps.reveal: In each region the largest of the candidate pressures is the physical one (the others are small corrections), so the boundary is where two candidates are equal. Example: the solar centre ($\rho=1.5\times10^5$, $T=1.6\times10^7$) lies far above the degeneracy line $T\approx6\times10^5$ K: ideal gas.
steps.explain: Pressures from different effects add, so whichever is largest dominates; equal values mark the crossover. Placing a known object (the solar centre) on the diagram is a good sanity check.

keyPoints: justification: equal pressures on a boundary

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.4: Lane–Emden solutions for $n=0$ and $n=1$
enc.goal: Solve $\dfrac1{\xi^2}\dfrac{d}{d\xi}\left(\xi^2\dfrac{d\theta}{d\xi}\right)=-\theta^n$ with $\theta=1$, $\theta'=0$ at $\xi=0$, analytically for $n=0$ and $n=1$ (hint for $n=1$: $\theta=\chi/\xi$ gives $\chi''=-\chi^n/\xi^{n-1}$).
given: $\theta^n\propto\rho$, the surface is the first zero $\xi_1$

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{d}{d\xi}(\xi^2\theta')=-\xi^2\Rightarrow\theta'=-\dfrac\xi3$ (the constant vanishes since $\theta'(0)=0$), $\theta=1-\dfrac{\xi^2}{6}$, $\xi_1=\sqrt6$.
steps.explain: $n=0$ means $\theta^0=1$: integrate $\frac{d}{d\xi}(\xi^2\theta')=-\xi^2$ once, $\xi^2\theta'=-\xi^3/3+C$, with $C=0$ for a regular centre. Integrate again. The surface is where $\theta=0$.

steps.reveal: $\xi^2\theta'=\xi\chi'-\chi$, so $\dfrac{d}{d\xi}(\xi^2\theta')=\xi\chi''$ and the equation becomes $\xi\chi''=-\xi^2(\chi/\xi)^n$, i.e. $\chi''=-\chi^n/\xi^{n-1}$.
steps.explain: Why this substitution: $\frac1{\xi^2}\frac{d}{d\xi}\xi^2\frac{d}{d\xi}$ is the radial part of the 3D Laplacian, and for any function $\frac{1}{\xi}\frac{d^2}{d\xi^2}(\xi\theta)$ equals it. So $\chi=\xi\theta$ turns it into a 1D second derivative (same trick as $u=r\psi$ for the hydrogen atom).

steps.reveal: $\chi''=-\chi\Rightarrow\chi=A\sin\xi+B\cos\xi$; $\theta$ finite at 0 needs $B=0$, $\theta(0)=1$ gives $A=1$: $\theta=\dfrac{\sin\xi}{\xi}$, $\xi_1=\pi$.
steps.explain: For $n=1$ that is the harmonic oscillator equation $\chi''=-\chi$. $\cos\xi/\xi$ blows up at the centre, so only $\sin\xi/\xi$ survives. First zero at $\pi$.

steps.reveal: Both have $\theta\approx1-\xi^2/6$ near the centre, as every Lane–Emden solution must (expand the equation at small $\xi$).
steps.explain: Near the centre expand $\theta=1+a\xi^2$: the left side gives $6a$, the right side $-1$, so $a=-\frac16$ for every $n$. A quick check of any solution.

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.5: Eddington’s standard model: $\beta$ against mass
enc.goal: If the gas pressure is a constant fraction $\beta$ of the total everywhere, show $P_{\rm tot}=\left(\dfrac{3\kappa_B^4}{a_B\mu^4m_H^4}\dfrac{1-\beta}{\beta^4}\right)^{1/3}\rho^{4/3}$. For stars of the same $\mu$, show $\dfrac{1-\beta}{\beta^4}=CM^2$, find $C$, and show that radiation pressure matters more in massive stars.

steps.reveal: From the gas law $T=\dfrac{\beta P\mu m_H}{\kappa_B\rho}$; put it into $P=\dfrac{a_BT^4}{3(1-\beta)}$: $P^3=\dfrac{3\kappa_B^4}{a_B\mu^4m_H^4}\dfrac{1-\beta}{\beta^4}\rho^4$. That is $P=K\rho^{4/3}$: a polytrope of index 3.
steps.explain: Two expressions for the same pressure: gas ($\beta P$) and radiation ($(1-\beta)P$). Solve the gas one for $T$ and insert it into the radiation one: $P^3\propto\rho^4$ with constant $\beta$. A polytrope with $n=3$ ($P\propto\rho^{1+1/n}$).

steps.prompt: Use the mass of an $n=3$ polytrope (it does not depend on $\rho_c$).
steps.reveal: $K^3=\dfrac{\pi^3G^3M^2}{(4\pi\times2.018)^2}$, so $\dfrac{1-\beta}{\beta^4}=CM^2$ with $C=\dfrac{\pi G^3a_B(\mu m_H)^4}{48\times2.018^2\,\kappa_B^4}$.
steps.explain: For $n=3$ the polytrope mass formula has no $\rho_c$ left: $M$ is fixed by $K$ alone. Invert to get $K$ as a function of $M$; equating with the $K(\beta)$ from step 1 links $\beta$ to $M$.

steps.reveal: $CM_\odot^2\approx4\times10^{-4}$. Solving the quartic: $\beta\approx1$ ($1M_\odot$), $0.966$ ($10M_\odot$), $0.573$ ($100M_\odot$).
steps.explain: Solve $\frac{1-\beta}{\beta^4}=CM^2$ numerically for each mass (it is a quartic in $\beta$; iterate or bisect between 0 and 1).

steps.reveal: $(1-\beta)/\beta^4$ grows as $M^2$: $\beta$ falls with mass, radiation pressure takes over in the most massive stars, which links to the Eddington limit (Exercise 3.5).
steps.explain: The left side grows as $\beta$ falls. More mass, larger right side, smaller $\beta$: radiation takes over the support of massive stars, consistent with the Eddington limit.

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.6: Chandrasekhar’s mass–radius relation (numerical)
enc.goal: Use the exact equation of state of Exercise 5.2 to solve the structure equation (5.13) for different central densities $\rho_c$. Plot $R(M)$ and show that $R\to0$ at the Chandrasekhar mass.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{dM_r}{dr}=4\pi r^2\rho$, $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=-\dfrac{GM_r\rho}{r^2}$, and $\dfrac{d\rho}{dr}=\dfrac{dP/dr}{dP/d\rho}$ with $dP/d\rho$ from $f(x)$.
steps.explain: A second-order equation is solved numerically as a system of first-order ones: mass inside $r$ and pressure. The equation of state links $P$ and $\rho$, so $d\rho/dr=(dP/dr)/(dP/d\rho)$.

steps.reveal: Start at small $r$ with $\rho=\rho_c$, $M_r=\frac43\pi r^3\rho_c$, integrate outward until $\rho=0$: that gives $R$ and $M=M_r(R)$. Repeat for $\rho_c$ from $10^8$ to $10^{14}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
steps.explain: Shooting outward: start just off the centre (where $M_r\approx\frac43\pi r^3\rho_c$, avoiding the $1/r^2$ singularity), step outward, and stop where the density reaches zero: that is the surface. Each $\rho_c$ gives one star, i.e. one point $(M,R)$.

steps.reveal: Low $\rho_c$: $R\propto M^{-1/3}$ (the $n=3/2$ polytrope). As $\rho_c\to\infty$ the electrons are relativistic everywhere, the star becomes an $n=3$ polytrope whose mass is fixed: $M_{\rm Ch}=4\pi\times2.018\,(K_2/\pi G)^{3/2}\approx1.44M_\odot$ for $\mu_e=2$, reached as $R\to0$ (Fig. 5.2).
steps.explain: Denser white dwarfs are smaller and heavier. As the electrons become relativistic the equation of state softens to $\rho^{4/3}$, and an $n=3$ polytrope can only have one mass: the curve approaches $M_{\rm Ch}$ as $R\to0$. Above it no equilibrium exists.

keyPoints: first-order system with $dP/d\rho$ from the exact EOS

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.7: Spin-up of the collapsing Sun
enc.goal: The Sun rotates in about $27$ days. If it collapsed to a white dwarf conserving angular momentum, what would the rotation period be? And for a neutron star?

steps.reveal: $I\Omega=$ const and $I\propto R^2$ give $P\propto R^2$: $P=P_\odot(R/R_\odot)^2$.
steps.explain: Angular momentum $I\Omega$ is conserved; with the same internal structure $I\propto MR^2$ and $M$ fixed, $\Omega\propto R^{-2}$, and the period $P=2\pi/\Omega\propto R^2$. Shrinking the radius 100 times speeds up the spin $10^4$ times, like a pirouetting skater.

steps.reveal: $P\approx27\ \mathrm d\times(6.4\times10^6/6.96\times10^8)^2\approx197$ s, a few minutes.
steps.explain: $(R_{\rm WD}/R_\odot)^2\approx8.5\times10^{-5}$; $27$ days is $2.3\times10^6$ s.

steps.reveal: $P\approx4.8\times10^{-4}$ s, i.e. half a millisecond, near the break-up limit; real pulsars are born slower because most angular momentum is lost on the way (winds, magnetic braking, mass loss).
steps.explain: $(10\,\mathrm{km}/R_\odot)^2\approx2\times10^{-10}$: sub-millisecond. That is about the fastest a neutron star can spin before the equator would fly apart, which shows angular momentum must be lost during collapse.

keyPoints: NS sub-millisecond, as a hint why pulsars spin fast

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.8: Spin-down power and magnetic field of the Crab pulsar
enc.goal: The Crab pulsar has $P=0.033$ s and $P/\dot P=2.5\times10^3$ yr. Estimate its energy loss rate and, using (5.35), its magnetic field.

steps.reveal: $\dot P=P/(2.5\times10^3\ \mathrm{yr})=4.2\times10^{-13}$; $I=1.1\times10^{38}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.
steps.explain: $P/\dot P$ is the characteristic age; convert years to seconds to get the dimensionless $\dot P$. $I=\frac25MR^2$ assumes a uniform sphere.

steps.reveal: $|\dot E|=I\Omega|\dot\Omega|=\dfrac{4\pi^2I\dot P}{P^3}\approx5.1\times10^{31}$ W, about $10^5L_\odot$: enough to power the Crab nebula.
steps.explain: Rotational energy $\frac12I\Omega^2$ with $\Omega=2\pi/P$: $\dot E=I\Omega\dot\Omega$ and $\dot\Omega=-2\pi\dot P/P^2$, so $|\dot E|=4\pi^2I\dot P/P^3$. The nebula's total emission matches this: the pulsar powers it.

steps.reveal: $B_p=\left(\dfrac{3\mu_0c^3I|\dot\Omega|}{2\pi R^6\Omega^3}\right)^{1/2}\approx8\times10^{8}$ T with $\sin\alpha=1$: about $10^8$–$10^9$ T, typical of young pulsars.
steps.explain: A rotating magnetic dipole radiates $\propto B^2\Omega^4$ (5.35). Equate to the measured spin-down loss and solve for $B$: about $10^8$ T, a trillion times the Earth's field (flux conservation during collapse amplifies it).

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.9: White-dwarf radius constant and the hottest brown dwarf
enc.goal: Find the proportionality constant in $R\propto M^{-1/3}$ (5.25) using $\xi_1=3.65$, $\xi_1^2|\theta'(\xi_1)|=2.71$ for $n=3/2$. For the limiting brown dwarf ($0.08M_\odot$) held up by electron degeneracy, estimate its radius, the thermal energy gained in its formation and its (uniform) temperature. Nuclear burning needs $T>10^7$ K.

steps.reveal: $\alpha=\dfrac{2.5K_1}{4\pi G}(4\pi\times2.71)^{1/3}M^{-1/3}$, so $R=3.65\,\alpha\approx8.8\times10^{6}\ \mathrm m\,(M/M_\odot)^{-1/3}$ for $\mu_e=2$: an Earth-sized white dwarf.
steps.explain: The polytrope formulas contain $\rho_c$ twice (in $\alpha$ and in $M$); eliminate it between them. For $n=\frac32$ what remains is $R\propto M^{-1/3}$: heavier white dwarfs are smaller.

steps.reveal: Then $R\approx4.9\times10^{7}$ m $\approx0.706R_J$ (Jupiter size, as observed for brown dwarfs).
steps.explain: A brown dwarf is mostly hydrogen, so more electrons per nucleon: $\mu_e=2/(1+X)$ instead of 2. Since $K_1\propto\mu_e^{-5/3}$ and $R\propto K_1M^{-1/3}$, it is larger for its mass than a white dwarf.

steps.reveal: $|E_G|=\frac67GM^2/R\approx2.9\times10^{40}$ J; by the virial theorem half of it stays as heat: $E_{\rm th}\approx1.5\times10^{40}$ J.
steps.explain: Polytrope binding energy $\frac{3}{5-n}\frac{GM^2}{R}$ ($\frac67$ for $n=\frac32$); the virial theorem keeps half of it as internal energy.

steps.reveal: $E_{\rm th}=\frac32\dfrac{M}{\mu m_H}\kappa_BT$ with $\mu\approx0.6$: $T\approx4.5\times10^{6}$ K, below $10^7$ K: the contraction is halted by degeneracy before hydrogen can ignite. That is why $\approx0.08M_\odot$ is the dividing line between stars and brown dwarfs.
steps.explain: Share that heat among $M/(\mu m_H)$ particles with $\frac32kT$ each. The answer stays below the $10^7$ K needed for hydrogen fusion: electron degeneracy stops the contraction first, so such an object never becomes a star.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.1: Star counts with a luminosity function and extinction
enc.goal: A fraction $\Phi(M)dM$ of stars has absolute magnitude in $[M,M+dM]$, absorption adds $a(r)$ magnitudes at distance $r$, and $D(r)$ is the number density. Show that the number of stars per unit apparent magnitude in solid angle $\omega$ is $A(m)=\omega\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\Phi[m+5-5\log_{10}r-a(r)]\,D(r)\,r^2dr$, and that it reduces to (6.3), $A\propto10^{0.6m}$, for equal stars, no absorption and uniform density.

steps.reveal: In $[r,r+dr]$ inside $\omega$ there are $\omega r^2D(r)\,dr$ stars.
steps.explain: A shell of radius $r$ and thickness $dr$ inside solid angle $\omega$ has volume $\omega r^2dr$; times the number density.

steps.prompt: Which of them have apparent magnitude in $[m,m+dm]$?
steps.reveal: Those with $M=m+5-5\log_{10}r-a(r)$; at fixed $r$, $dM=dm$, so the fraction is $\Phi(m+5-5\log_{10}r-a)\,dm$. Summing over shells gives the formula.
steps.explain: A star at distance $r$ appears with magnitude $m$ only if its absolute magnitude is $M=m-5\log_{10}r+5-a(r)$; the luminosity function gives the fraction of stars with that $M$. Add up all shells.

steps.reveal: $\delta(g(r))$ with $g=m+5-5\log_{10}r-M_0$ picks $r_0=10^{(m-M_0+5)/5}$ with weight $1/|g'(r_0)|=r_0\ln10/5$: $A(m)=\dfrac{\omega D\ln10}{5}r_0^3\propto10^{0.6m}$, which is (6.3).
steps.explain: Delta functions of a function: $\delta(g(r))=\delta(r-r_0)/|g'(r_0)|$. Here $g'=-\frac{5}{r\ln10}$. Then $A\propto r_0^3$ and $r_0\propto10^{m/5}$, so $A\propto10^{3m/5}=10^{0.6m}$. Each step fainter by one magnitude reaches $10^{0.2}$ times farther, i.e. $10^{0.6}$ times more volume.

steps.reveal: Deviations from $10^{0.6m}$ tell us about $D(r)$ (the structure of the Galaxy) or $a(r)$ (extinction), the basis of statistical astronomy (Kapteyn).
steps.explain: If counts grow more slowly than $10^{0.6m}$, either the density falls off with distance or dust dims the distant stars: counts probe the structure of the Galaxy.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.2: Extinction as an exponential
enc.goal: The interstellar medium dims stars in the disk by about $1.5$ magnitudes per kpc. Show that brightness then falls as $e^{-\alpha r}/r^2$ and find $\alpha$.

steps.prompt: Flux reduction factor from $\Delta m=1.5\,r$ (r in kpc).
steps.reveal: $F/F_0=10^{-0.4\times1.5r}=e^{-0.6\ln10\,r}$, times the geometric $1/r^2$.
steps.explain: Magnitudes to flux: $F/F_0=10^{-0.4\Delta m}$, and $10^y=e^{y\ln10}$. With $\Delta m=1.5r$ that is $e^{-0.6\ln10\,r}$. Multiply by the usual $1/r^2$.

steps.reveal: $\alpha=0.6\ln10\approx1.38\ \mathrm{kpc^{-1}}=4.5\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
steps.explain: $\alpha=0.6\ln10=1.38$ per kpc; convert kpc to m.

steps.reveal: The optical depth is $\tau=\alpha r\approx1.4$ per kpc: the galactic centre ($8$ kpc, $\tau\approx11$, about 30 magnitudes) is invisible in visible light.
steps.explain: $\alpha r$ is the optical depth. Toward the Galactic centre it is ~11: a factor $e^{-11}$, so the centre is only seen in infrared and radio, where dust absorbs much less.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.3: Oort constants in a Keplerian region
enc.goal: If the gravitational field falls as $r^{-2}$, find the Oort constants $A$ and $B$ (6.21), (6.22). Show that the epicyclic frequency equals the angular velocity and explain its significance.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{\Theta^2}{R}=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}\Rightarrow\omega\propto R^{-3/2}$, $\dfrac{d\omega}{dR}=-\dfrac32\dfrac\omega R$.
steps.explain: Kepler region: all mass inside, so $\Theta^2/R=GM/R^2$, $\Theta\propto R^{-1/2}$ and $\omega=\Theta/R\propto R^{-3/2}$. Differentiating a power law: $\frac{d\omega}{dR}=-\frac32\frac\omega R$.

steps.reveal: $A=\frac34\omega_0$, $B=A-\omega_0=-\frac14\omega_0$.
steps.explain: Insert into the definitions: $A=-\frac12R(-\frac32\frac\omega R)=\frac34\omega$, $B=A-\omega$.

steps.reveal: $\kappa^2=-4B\omega_0=\omega_0^2$, so $\kappa=\omega_0$.
steps.explain: Plug into $\kappa^2=-4B\omega_0$ ($A-B=\omega_0$).

steps.reveal: The radial oscillation has the same period as the orbit: the perturbed orbit closes after one revolution. It is a Kepler ellipse, as it must be for an inverse-square force. In the flat-rotation-curve Galaxy $\kappa=\sqrt2\,\omega$ and orbits are rosettes.
steps.explain: Closed orbits: a star slightly off a circular orbit oscillates in radius with $\kappa$ while circling with $\omega$. If they are equal, the oscillation repeats exactly each orbit: an ellipse. In a flat rotation curve $\kappa\ne\omega$, so the ellipse precesses and the orbit is a rosette.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.4: Vertical oscillations through the galactic disk
enc.goal: Model the disk as an infinite slab of constant density. Show that a star displaced vertically oscillates harmonically about the mid-plane. For a mid-plane density of $5\times10^6$ hydrogen atoms per $\mathrm{m^3}$ estimate the period and compare with the orbital period near the Sun.

steps.reveal: $g_z=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dz}=-4\pi G\rho z$ (Gauss’s law with a pillbox, symmetric about $z=0$).
steps.explain: Gauss's law for a slab: a box (pillbox) from $-z$ to $z$ encloses mass $\rho\cdot2z$ per area; by symmetry the field points to the mid-plane and has the same size on both faces. So $2g\,A=4\pi G\rho\cdot2zA$: $g=4\pi G\rho z$, growing linearly like a spring.

steps.reveal: $\ddot z=-4\pi G\rho z$: simple harmonic with $\omega_z^2=4\pi G\rho$.
steps.explain: A restoring force proportional to the displacement is a harmonic oscillator: $\omega_z^2=4\pi G\rho$, the "spring constant per mass".

steps.reveal: $\rho=8.4\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$: $P_z=2\pi/\sqrt{4\pi G\rho}\approx7.5\times10^{7}$ yr; the orbit takes $2\pi\times8\ \mathrm{kpc}/220\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\approx2.2\times10^{8}$ yr.
steps.explain: Convert atoms per m$^3$ to kg/m$^3$ ($\times1.67\times10^{-27}$). $P=2\pi/\omega_z$; for the orbit: circumference over speed.

steps.reveal: A star crosses the disk a few times per orbit; the Sun is now about $20$ pc above the plane, moving up.
steps.explain: The vertical period is shorter than the orbital one, so stars bob up and down through the disk a few times per orbit.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.5: Oscillator strength and the Einstein $B$ coefficient
enc.goal: The oscillator strength of §2.7 satisfies $\dfrac{e^2}{4\epsilon_0m_e}f=h\nu_0B_{lu}$. Show that this makes the discussions of §2.7 and §6.6 consistent.

steps.reveal: Visible lines through cold gas: $h\nu_0\gg\kappa_BT$, so stimulated emission is negligible and the bracket is 1; also $n_l\approx n$.
steps.explain: The two formulas describe the same absorption in two languages. §2.7 ignored stimulated emission: fine when $h\nu\gg kT$ because the Boltzmann factor $e^{-h\nu/kT}$ is tiny and almost all atoms are in the lower level.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{h\nu_0}{c}nB_{lu}\phi=\dfrac{e^2}{4\epsilon_0m_ec}nf\phi$ exactly when $\dfrac{e^2}{4\epsilon_0m_e}f=h\nu_0B_{lu}$.
steps.explain: Set the two expressions for $\alpha_\nu$ equal; $n$, $\phi$ and $c$ cancel, leaving the stated relation.

steps.reveal: $f$ (classical oscillator language) and $B_{lu}$ (quantum transition rate) are the same physics; the radio case (21 cm, $h\nu_0\ll\kappa_BT$) needs the full bracket of (6.65).
steps.explain: For radio lines ($h u\ll kT$) the bracket $1-e^{-h u/kT}\approx h u/kT$ is small: stimulated emission nearly cancels absorption, and the full formula is needed.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.6: Three-level atom and population inversion
enc.goal: An atom has levels 1, 2, 3 and no transitions between 2 and 3. Using balance equations like (6.59) and neglecting radiative excitation, show $\dfrac{n_3}{n_2}=\dfrac{g_3(1+A_{21}/n_e\gamma_{21})}{g_2(1+A_{31}/n_e\gamma_{31})}e^{-E_{23}/\kappa_BT}$. Discuss when the populations are inverted.

steps.prompt: Balance for each upper level separately (they only talk to level 1).
steps.explain: Statistical equilibrium: for each level, the rate in = the rate out. Level 2 is filled only by collisions from level 1 and empties by spontaneous decay and collisions back to 1. The same for level 3, separately, because 2 and 3 do not connect.

Divide the two balances: $n_1$ and $n_e$ cancel. Detailed balance turns the upward collision rates into downward ones times $\frac{g_u}{g_l}e^{-E/kT}$, which brings in the Boltzmann factor between 2 and 3.

steps.reveal: $n_e\gamma\gg A$: the fractions $\to1$ and we recover Boltzmann.
steps.explain: At high density collisions dominate over spontaneous emission, the $A$ terms drop out, and the ratio is the Boltzmann one: the gas is in LTE.

steps.reveal: Needs $\dfrac{1+A_{21}/n_e\gamma_{21}}{1+A_{31}/n_e\gamma_{31}}>e^{E_{23}/\kappa_BT}$: level 2 must drain radiatively much faster than level 3 ($A_{21}/\gamma_{21}\gg A_{31}/\gamma_{31}$) at a density where $A_{21}\gtrsim n_e\gamma_{21}$. Collisions pump both levels, but 2 empties quickly: that is the principle behind interstellar masers.
steps.explain: Inversion needs the correction factor to beat the Boltzmann factor: level 2 must empty much faster (large $A_{21}$) than level 3, so atoms pile up in 3. With more atoms (per state) in 3 than in 2, radiation at the 3→2 frequency is amplified instead of absorbed: a maser.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.7: Rotational lines of CO
enc.goal: CO emits at integer multiples of $115$ GHz. With $I$ the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the molecule, show $E_J=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2I}J(J+1)$ and that the selection rule $\Delta J=-1$ gives the observed spectrum. Estimate the C–O distance.

steps.reveal: A rigid rotor has $E=L^2/2I$ and $L^2=\hbar^2J(J+1)$: $E_J=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2I}J(J+1)$.
steps.explain: A rigid rotor has only rotational kinetic energy $L^2/2I$; quantising $L^2=\hbar^2J(J+1)$ gives the levels.

steps.reveal: $E_J-E_{J-1}=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{I}J$, so $\nu_J=\dfrac{\hbar}{2\pi I}J$: equally spaced, $J\times115$ GHz.
steps.explain: Energy difference of neighbours: $J(J+1)-(J-1)J=2J$, so $\Delta E=\frac{\hbar^2}{I}J$ and $\nu=\Delta E/h=\frac{\hbar J}{2\pi I}$. Lines at $J$ times a basic frequency: the 115 GHz spacing gives $I$.

steps.prompt: Moment of inertia and bond length.
steps.reveal: $I=\dfrac{\hbar}{2\pi\times115\ \mathrm{GHz}}=1.5\times10^{-46}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$; with the reduced mass $m=\frac{12\times16}{28}u=1.1\times10^{-26}$ kg, $r=\sqrt{I/m}\approx1.1\times10^{-10}$ m $\approx1.1$ Å.
steps.explain: For two masses, $I=m_{\rm red}r^2$ with the reduced mass $\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}$; solve for $r$. About 1 Å, a typical chemical bond.

enc.title: Choudhuri 7.1: Jeans theorem
enc.goal: If $K(\mathbf x,\mathbf v)$ is a constant of motion (energy, angular momentum), show that $f(K)$ is a time-independent solution of the collisionless Boltzmann equation.
given: collisionless Boltzmann: $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla f-\nabla\Phi\cdot\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial\mathbf v}=0$, i.e. $df/dt=0$ along orbits

steps.reveal:
$\partial f/\partial t=0$ and $\mathbf v\cdot
abla f-
abla\Phi\cdot\partial_{\mathbf v}f=f'(K)\left(\mathbf v\cdot
abla K-
abla\Phi\cdot\partial_{\mathbf v}Kight)$.
steps.explain: If $f$ depends on $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf v$ only through $K$, the chain rule gives $\nabla f=f'(K)\nabla K$ and $\partial_{\mathbf v}f=f'(K)\partial_{\mathbf v}K$. Factor out $f'(K)$.

steps.reveal: It is $dK/dt$ along an orbit ($\dot{\mathbf x}=\mathbf v$, $\dot{\mathbf v}=-\nabla\Phi$), which vanishes for a constant of motion.
steps.explain: Along an orbit $\dot{\mathbf x}=\mathbf v$ and $\dot{\mathbf v}=-\nabla\Phi$, so the bracket is exactly $\frac{dK}{dt}=\dot{\mathbf x}\cdot\nabla K+\dot{\mathbf v}\cdot\partial_{\mathbf v}K$. A constant of motion has $dK/dt=0$.

steps.reveal: Any function of integrals of motion is a steady state; e.g. $f(E)$ gives isotropic spherical systems, $f(E,L_z)$ axisymmetric ones (the converse statement is the strong Jeans theorem).
steps.explain: So building equilibrium galaxy or cluster models reduces to choosing a function of $E$ (and $L$). Which integrals you use decides the symmetry of the model.

enc.title: Choudhuri 7.2: Continuity equation from the CBE in cylindrical coordinates
enc.goal: Write the collisionless Boltzmann equation in cylindrical coordinates and, with no assumptions, integrate over velocity space to show $\dfrac{\partial n}{\partial t}+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial r}(n\langle\Pi\rangle)+\dfrac1r\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(n\langle\Theta\rangle)+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}(n\langle Z\rangle)+\dfrac{n\langle\Pi\rangle}{r}=0$.

steps.reveal: $\partial_tf+\Pi\partial_rf+\dfrac\Theta r\partial_\theta f+Z\partial_zf+\left(\dfrac{\Theta^2}{r}-\partial_r\Phi\right)\partial_\Pi f-\left(\dfrac{\Pi\Theta}{r}+\dfrac1r\partial_\theta\Phi\right)\partial_\Theta f-\partial_z\Phi\,\partial_Zf=0$; the $\Theta^2/r$ and $\Pi\Theta/r$ terms are the centrifugal and Coriolis terms of $\dot\Pi$ and $\dot\Theta$.
steps.explain: In cylindrical coordinates the velocity components change along an orbit even without forces, because the basis vectors rotate. These "fictitious" accelerations are $\dot\Pi\ni\Theta^2/r$ (centrifugal) and $\dot\Theta\ni-\Pi\Theta/r$ (Coriolis); they appear as coefficients of the velocity derivatives.

steps.reveal: They give $\partial_tn+\partial_r(n\langle\Pi\rangle)+\frac1r\partial_\theta(n\langle\Theta\rangle)+\partial_z(n\langle Z\rangle)$.
steps.explain: Integrating $f$ over velocities gives $n$; integrating $\Pi f$ gives $n\langle\Pi\rangle$. Space and time derivatives can be pulled out of the velocity integral.

steps.prompt: Integrate the acceleration terms by parts ($f\to0$ at large speed).
steps.reveal: Potential terms and $\frac{\Theta^2}{r}\partial_\Pi f$ integrate to zero (coefficient independent of $\Pi$). But $-\displaystyle\int\frac{\Pi\Theta}{r}\partial_\Theta f\,d^3v=+\frac1r\int\Pi f\,d^3v=\frac{n\langle\Pi\rangle}{r}$.
steps.explain: By parts in velocity space: $\int g\,\partial_\Pi f\,d\Pi=-\int f\,\partial_\Pi g\,d\Pi$ (no boundary term, $f\to0$). If $g$ does not depend on $\Pi$, the result is 0. The Coriolis coefficient $\Pi\Theta/r$ depends on $\Theta$, and $\partial_\Theta(\Pi\Theta/r)=\Pi/r$ leaves the extra term $n\langle\Pi\rangle/r$.

steps.reveal: It is the continuity equation $\partial_tn+\nabla\cdot(n\langle\mathbf v\rangle)=0$ written in cylindrical coordinates: $\frac1r\partial_r(rn\langle\Pi\rangle)=\partial_r(n\langle\Pi\rangle)+\frac{n\langle\Pi\rangle}r$.
steps.explain: In cylindrical coordinates the divergence has $\frac1r\partial_r(r\,\cdot)$, which by the product rule contains exactly that extra $\frac{n\langle\Pi\rangle}{r}$: it is just the continuity equation.

keyPoints: centrifugal and Coriolis terms in the CBE

enc.title: Choudhuri 7.3: Moments of the CBE: fluid equations for stars
enc.goal: From $\partial_tf+v_i\partial_{x_i}f+\dfrac{F_i}m\partial_{v_i}f=0$ show (2) $\partial_t(nm)+\partial_{x_i}(nm\langle v_i\rangle)=0$; multiplying by $mv_j$, (3) $\partial_t(nm\langle v_j\rangle)+\partial_{x_i}(nm\langle v_iv_j\rangle)-nF_j=0$; with $P_{ij}=nm\langle(v_i-\langle v_i\rangle)(v_j-\langle v_j\rangle)\rangle$ show (5) $nm\left(\partial_t\langle v_j\rangle+\langle v_i\rangle\partial_{x_i}\langle v_j\rangle\right)=-\partial_{x_i}P_{ji}+nF_j$. Do (2) and (5) look like fluid equations?

steps.reveal: $\int d^3v$ of the equation: the force term vanishes, giving (2).
steps.explain: Moments: integrate the equation over all velocities. The force term is a total derivative in $v$, which integrates to zero; what is left is mass conservation.

steps.reveal: Multiply by $mv_j$ and integrate: $\int mv_jF_i/m\,\partial_{v_i}f=-F_jn$, giving (3).
steps.explain: Multiply by $mv_j$ first. Now by parts the force term gives $-F_j\int f=-nF_j$ (the derivative hits $v_j$). This is momentum balance.

steps.reveal: $\langle v_iv_j\rangle=\langle v_i\rangle\langle v_j\rangle+P_{ij}/nm$. Expand (3) and subtract $\langle v_j\rangle\times$(2): the terms $\langle v_j\rangle[\partial_t(nm)+\partial_i(nm\langle v_i\rangle)]$ cancel, leaving (5).
steps.explain: Split velocities into mean + random: $\langle v_iv_j\rangle=\langle v_i\rangle\langle v_j\rangle+$ dispersion. The dispersion part is the pressure tensor. Subtracting $\langle v_j\rangle$ times the continuity equation removes the time derivative of the density, leaving "mass × acceleration = forces".

steps.reveal: (2) is the continuity equation, (5) the Euler equation with an anisotropic pressure tensor $P_{ij}$ from velocity dispersion: the stellar "Jeans equations". Unlike a gas, nothing closes them (no equation of state), because stars do not collide.
steps.explain: For a gas, collisions make $P_{ij}$ isotropic and an equation of state closes the system. Stars never collide, so the dispersion can be different in different directions and there is no equation of state: one more moment always appears (the closure problem).

keyPoints: integration by parts of the force term
continuity + Euler analogy and the closure problem

enc.title: Choudhuri 7.4: The King model
enc.goal: Take $f=A\left[e^{-\beta E}-1\right]$ for $E<0$ and $f=0$ for $E>0$, $E=\frac12v^2+\Phi$, $\Phi\to0$ at infinity. Find $\rho(r)$ (it involves the error function), write the equation replacing (7.19), solve it for $-\beta\Phi(0)=12,9,6,3$ and show that $\rho$ vanishes at a finite radius.

steps.reveal: $\displaystyle\int_0^{v_e}4\pi v^2e^{-\beta v^2/2}dv=\left(\frac{2\pi}\beta\right)^{3/2}\left[\mathrm{erf}\sqrt W-\sqrt{\frac{4W}\pi}e^{-W}\right]$ and $\int_0^{v_e}4\pi v^2dv=\frac{4\pi}3v_e^3$, so $\rho=A\left(\dfrac{2\pi}\beta\right)^{3/2}\left[e^W\mathrm{erf}\sqrt W-\sqrt{\dfrac{4W}\pi}\left(1+\dfrac{2W}3\right)\right]$.
steps.explain: Only stars with $E<0$ are bound, so integrate up to the escape speed $v_e$. The $e^{-\beta v^2/2}$ part is a truncated Gaussian integral (that is where erf comes from), the $-1$ part is just the volume of a velocity sphere.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac1{r^2}\dfrac{d}{dr}\left(r^2\dfrac{dW}{dr}\right)=-4\pi G\beta\rho(W)$, with $W(0)=W_0$, $W'(0)=0$. In units of $r_0=\sqrt{9/(4\pi G\beta\rho_c)}$ the right side is $-9\rho(W)/\rho(W_0)$.
steps.explain: Poisson's equation with the density as a function of the potential gives one ordinary differential equation for $W(r)$. Choosing units built from the central density makes it dimensionless, with $W_0$ the only parameter.

steps.reveal: Integrating outward, $W$ (and $\rho$) reach zero at the tidal radius $r_t/r_0\approx4.7$, $18$, $131$, $548$ for $W_0=3,6,9,12$.
steps.explain: Integrate outward from the centre (regular start $W'=0$); where $W$ hits 0 the density is zero: the edge of the cluster (tidal radius).

steps.reveal: Subtracting the constant removes the stars with $E\ge0$ (they escape), so the mass is finite, unlike the isothermal sphere (7.16) with $\rho\propto r^{-2}$ forever. Larger $W_0$ means a more concentrated cluster: King models fit globular clusters well.
steps.explain: The isothermal sphere has stars of all energies and falls off only like $r^{-2}$ (infinite mass). Removing the unbound stars gives a finite cluster, which is what tidal fields of the Galaxy do to real globular clusters.

enc.title: Choudhuri 8.2: Shearing a frozen-in field
enc.goal: A uniform field $\mathbf B=B_0\hat e_y$ sits in a perfectly conducting plasma. At $t=0$ the flow $\mathbf v=v_0e^{-y^2}\hat e_x$ is switched on. Find $\mathbf B(t)$ and sketch the field lines.
given: ideal induction equation $\partial_t\mathbf B=\nabla\times(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)$

steps.reveal: $v_x\hat e_x\times(B_x\hat e_x+B_0\hat e_y)=v_0e^{-y^2}B_0\hat e_z$ ($B_x$ adds nothing since $\mathbf v\parallel\hat e_x$).
steps.explain: Cross product with $\hat e_x\times\hat e_x=0$ and $\hat e_x\times\hat e_y=\hat e_z$.

steps.reveal: $\nabla\times(F(y)\hat e_z)=F'(y)\hat e_x$: $\partial_tB_x=-2yv_0B_0e^{-y^2}$, $\partial_tB_y=0$.
steps.explain: The curl of $F(y)\hat e_z$ has only an $x$ component, $\partial_yF$. Here $F=v_0B_0e^{-y^2}$, so $F'=-2yv_0B_0e^{-y^2}$.

steps.reveal: $\mathbf B=B_0\hat e_y-2v_0B_0t\,ye^{-y^2}\hat e_x$: $B_x$ grows linearly in time.
steps.explain: The right side does not depend on time (it involves only $B_y$, which stays $B_0$), so integrate trivially: $B_x$ grows linearly in $t$.

steps.reveal: $dx/dy=B_x/B_y=-2v_0t\,ye^{-y^2}$, i.e. $x=x_0+v_0te^{-y^2}$: each line is the initial straight line displaced by the fluid, a bump that moves to $+x$ around $y=0$ and grows. Flux freezing: the lines move with the plasma.
steps.explain: A field line follows $\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{B_x}{B_y}$; integrating gives the displacement $v_0te^{-y^2}$, exactly how far the fluid at height $y$ has moved. The field lines are carried with the flow (frozen in), and stretching them builds up $B_x$: the basic dynamo ingredient.

enc.title: Choudhuri 8.3: Pressure in a current-carrying plasma column
enc.goal: A cylindrical plasma column carries a uniform current density $j\hat e_z$. Find $B_\theta(r)$; from (8.29) show the static equilibrium $\dfrac{d}{dr}\left(P+\dfrac{B_\theta^2}{2\mu_0}\right)+\dfrac{B_\theta^2}{\mu_0r}=0$, and find $P(r)$.

steps.reveal: $2\pi rB_\theta=\mu_0j\pi r^2\Rightarrow B_\theta=\dfrac{\mu_0jr}2$ inside.
steps.explain: Ampère with a circle of radius $r$ inside the column: by symmetry $B_\theta$ is the same all around, so the left side is $2\pi rB_\theta$, and the enclosed current is $j\pi r^2$. The field grows linearly inside (like $g$ inside a uniform planet).

steps.reveal:
$\dfrac1{\mu_0}(
abla	imes\mathbf B)	imes\mathbf B=-
abla\dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0}+\dfrac{(\mathbf B\cdot
abla)\mathbf B}{\mu_0}$ and $(\mathbf B\cdot
abla)\mathbf B=-\dfrac{B_	heta^2}r\hat e_r$ (curvature of circular field lines): the stated equation.
steps.explain: The Lorentz force in two parts: a magnetic pressure gradient $- abla(B^2/2\mu_0)$ and a magnetic tension $(\mathbf B\cdot abla)\mathbf B/\mu_0$. For circular field lines the tension points inward with size $B^2/(\mu_0r)$, like a rubber band around a bundle. Balance with $- abla P$ gives the equation.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{d}{dr}\dfrac{B_\theta^2}{2\mu_0}=\dfrac{\mu_0j^2r}4$ and $\dfrac{B_\theta^2}{\mu_0r}=\dfrac{\mu_0j^2r}4$, so $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=-\dfrac{\mu_0j^2r}2$, $P=\dfrac{\mu_0j^2}4(a^2-r^2)$ with $P(a)=0$.
steps.explain: Insert $B_\theta=\mu_0jr/2$: both magnetic terms equal $\mu_0j^2r/4$, so $dP/dr=-\mu_0j^2r/2$. Integrate from the surface ($P=0$) inward.

steps.reveal: Magnetic pressure plus tension squeeze the column (the pinch), balanced by the gas pressure; this equilibrium is violently unstable (sausage and kink modes).
steps.explain: The current's own field squeezes the plasma; the pressure peaks on the axis. This is the "pinch" used in fusion experiments, and its instabilities are why tokamaks need an extra axial field.

enc.title: Choudhuri 8.4: Alfvén waves
enc.goal: Perturb a uniform field $B_0$ in an ideal plasma, neglecting pressure and gravity: $\rho\dfrac{d\mathbf v}{dt}=\dfrac{(\nabla\times\mathbf B)\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}$. Show that the perturbations travel along $\mathbf B_0$ at $v_A=B_0/\sqrt{\mu_0\rho}$.

steps.prompt: Linearise with $\mathbf B=B_0\hat e_z+\mathbf b$, transverse $\mathbf v=v_x(z,t)\hat e_x$, $\mathbf b=b_x(z,t)\hat e_x$.
steps.reveal: Induction: $\partial_tb_x=B_0\partial_zv_x$. Momentum: $(\nabla\times\mathbf b)\times B_0\hat e_z=B_0\partial_zb_x\hat e_x$, so $\rho\partial_tv_x=\dfrac{B_0}{\mu_0}\partial_zb_x$.
steps.explain: Linearise: keep only terms first order in the small $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf b$. In the induction equation $\mathbf v\times B_0\hat e_z$ has a $y$ component $-v_xB_0$, and its curl gives $\partial_tb_x=B_0\partial_zv_x$. In the force, only $\nabla\times\mathbf b$ crossed with the background $B_0$ survives.

steps.reveal: $\partial_t^2v_x=\dfrac{B_0^2}{\mu_0\rho}\partial_z^2v_x$: a wave along $\mathbf B_0$ with speed $v_A=\dfrac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0\rho}}$.
steps.explain: Differentiate the momentum equation in time and insert the induction equation for $\partial_tb_x$: a wave equation $\partial_t^2v=v_A^2\partial_z^2v$. Speed$^2$ = tension/(mass density), like a string.

steps.reveal: Field lines behave like strings under tension $B^2/\mu_0$ loaded with the plasma mass: plucked strings. In the ISM ($B\sim10^{-10}$ T, $n\sim10^6\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$) $v_A\sim2\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
steps.explain: Plug in numbers: $v_A=B/\sqrt{\mu_0\rho}$ with $\rho=nm_H$. Alfvén waves carry energy along field lines (e.g. heating the solar corona).

enc.title: Choudhuri 8.5: Rise speed of a buoyant flux tube
enc.goal: A horizontal flux tube (field $B$, radius $a$) lies in an isothermal atmosphere with constant $g$ and scale height $\Lambda=P/\rho g$. The drag per unit length is $\frac12C_D\rho v^2a$. Show that it rises at the asymptotic speed $v_A\left(\dfrac{\pi a}{\Lambda C_D}\right)^{1/2}$, $v_A=B/\sqrt{\mu_0\rho}$.

steps.reveal: Same $T$ means $\rho\propto P$: $\dfrac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}=\dfrac{P_e-P_i}{P_e}=\dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0P}$.
steps.explain: The tube is in pressure balance with its surroundings, but part of its inside pressure is magnetic, so the gas pressure inside is lower. At the same temperature lower gas pressure means lower density: the tube is lighter than its surroundings.

steps.reveal: $\Delta\rho\,g\pi a^2=\dfrac{\rho gB^2}{2\mu_0P}\pi a^2=\dfrac{\pi a^2B^2}{2\mu_0\Lambda}$.
steps.explain: Archimedes: buoyant force = (density deficit) × $g$ × volume ($\pi a^2$ per unit length). Use $\rho g/P=1/\Lambda$.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{\pi a^2B^2}{2\mu_0\Lambda}=\dfrac12C_D\rho v^2a\Rightarrow v^2=\dfrac{B^2}{\mu_0\rho}\dfrac{\pi a}{\Lambda C_D}$, the stated result.
steps.explain: Terminal velocity: it accelerates until drag equals buoyancy. Solve for $v$; $B^2/\mu_0\rho$ is $v_A^2$.

steps.reveal: Magnetic buoyancy brings tubes generated by the solar dynamo to the surface, where they form sunspots.
steps.explain: Strong fields produced deep inside rise to the surface within months, which is how sunspots appear.

enc.title: Choudhuri 8.6: Relativistic Fermi acceleration
enc.goal: (Special relativity.) A relativistic particle moving in one dimension is reflected by reflectors moving with speeds $\pm U$. Show that the average energy gain per collision is (8.44), $\Delta E_{\rm ave}=4\left(\dfrac Uc\right)^2E$.
given: Lorentz transformation of energy for $v\approx c$: $E'=\gamma E(1\pm\beta)$, $\beta=U/c$

steps.reveal: Transform into the reflector frame, reverse the momentum, transform back: $E_+=\gamma^2(1+\beta)^2E=\dfrac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}E$.
steps.explain: Reflection is simple in the reflector's frame: energy unchanged, momentum reversed. So transform into that frame (gain a Doppler factor $\gamma(1+\beta)$), reflect, transform back (another $\gamma(1+\beta)$). With $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ the product is $\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}$.

steps.reveal: $E_-=\dfrac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}E$.
steps.explain: Same with $\beta\to-\beta$: a loss.

steps.reveal: Head-on collisions are more frequent: rates $\propto c+U$ and $c-U$, probabilities $\frac{1\pm\beta}2$.
steps.explain: A particle meets approaching reflectors more often: relative speed $c+U$ versus $c-U$. So gains are slightly more frequent than losses.

steps.reveal: $\Delta E_{\rm ave}=\dfrac{1+\beta}2\dfrac{2\beta}{1-\beta}E-\dfrac{1-\beta}2\dfrac{2\beta}{1+\beta}E=\dfrac{4\beta^2}{1-\beta^2}E=4\gamma^2\beta^2E\approx4\left(\dfrac Uc\right)^2E$: second-order Fermi acceleration.
steps.explain: Average the relative changes weighted by these probabilities: first-order terms in $\beta$ cancel, a $\beta^2$ remains. A slow, net energy gain: second-order Fermi acceleration of cosmic rays.

keyPoints: energy after head-on and overtaking reflections
