enc.title: Choudhuri 8.8: Pulsar dispersion from the plasma dispersion relation
enc.goal: From $\omega^2=\omega_p^2+k^2c^2$ (8.82) show $v_{gr}=c\sqrt{1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2}$. With $T_a=\displaystyle\int_0^L\frac{ds}{v_{gr}}$ and $\omega_p\ll\omega$, show that signals of different frequency are dispersed as in (6.68), $\dfrac{dT_a}{d\omega}=-\dfrac{e^2}{\epsilon_0m_ec\,\omega^3}\displaystyle\int n_e\,ds$.

steps.reveal: $2\omega\,d\omega=2c^2k\,dk\Rightarrow v_{gr}=\dfrac{c^2k}\omega=c\sqrt{1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2}$ (always $<c$).
steps.explain: Differentiate the dispersion relation: $2\omega\,d\omega=2c^2k\,dk$, so $d\omega/dk=c^2k/\omega$; express $k$ through $\omega$ with the same relation. Below $\omega_p$ there is no real $k$: radio waves below the plasma frequency cannot propagate.

steps.reveal: $T_a=\displaystyle\int\frac{ds}{c}\left(1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}\right)^{-1/2}\approx\frac Lc+\frac{1}{2c\omega^2}\int\omega_p^2ds=\frac Lc+\frac{e^2}{2\epsilon_0m_ec\,\omega^2}\int n_e\,ds$.
steps.explain: Expand $(1-\epsilon)^{-1/2}\approx1+\frac\epsilon2$ for small $\epsilon=\omega_p^2/\omega^2$, and write $\omega_p^2\propto n_e$.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{dT_a}{d\omega}=-\dfrac{e^2}{\epsilon_0m_ec\,\omega^3}\displaystyle\int n_e\,ds$ (6.68): low frequencies arrive later; measuring the delay gives the dispersion measure $\int n_e\,ds$, hence pulsar distances.
steps.explain: Differentiate with respect to $\omega$: $\frac{d}{d\omega}\omega^{-2}=-2\omega^{-3}$. Low frequencies arrive later. Measuring the sweep of a pulse across frequencies gives $\int n_e\,ds$, and with a model of the Galaxy's electron density, the distance.

enc.title: Choudhuri 9.1: Total light of a de Vaucouleurs galaxy
enc.goal: An elliptical galaxy appears circular with the de Vaucouleurs profile $I(r)=I_e\exp\left\{-7.67\left[(r/r_e)^{1/4}-1\right]\right\}$ (9.2). Show that the total light $\int_0^\infty I\,2\pi r\,dr=7.22\pi r_e^2I_e$, and that exactly half comes from within $r_e$.

steps.reveal: $r=r_eu^4$, $dr=4r_eu^3du$: $L=2\pi r_e^2I_ee^{b}\displaystyle\int_0^\infty4u^7e^{-bu}du$ with $b=7.67$.
steps.explain: Total light of a round galaxy = surface brightness integrated over rings of area $2\pi r\,dr$. The awkward $r^{1/4}$ suggests $u=(r/r_e)^{1/4}$: $r=r_eu^4$, and $r\,dr=4r_e^2u^7du$.
$\int_0^\infty u^7e^{-bu}du=7!/b^8$ (a Gamma function). The rest is arithmetic: $8e^{7.67}\cdot5040/7.67^8\approx7.2$.

steps.reveal: Fraction $=\gamma(8,b)/7!=0.5$: one half. That is why $b=7.67$: it is chosen so that $r_e$ is the half-light (effective) radius.
steps.explain: Up to $r_e$ means $u\le1$: the same integral cut off at 1 (an incomplete Gamma function). The constant 7.67 was chosen precisely so that this is half: $r_e$ is the half-light radius by construction.

enc.title: Choudhuri 9.2: Faber–Jackson slope from Fig. 9.5
enc.goal: From Figure 9.5 argue that $\sigma\propto L^\alpha$ and estimate $\alpha$.
given: on a log–log plot a power law is a straight line with slope $\alpha$
Note: Read the actual points in Fig. 9.5 of the book; the slope there should come out near $1/4$.

steps.reveal: Plot (or read) $\log\sigma$ against $\log L$ (or absolute magnitude, $\log L=-0.4M+$ const): the ellipticals lie along a straight band.
steps.explain: A power law $\sigma\propto L^\alpha$ becomes $\log\sigma=\alpha\log L+$ const: a straight line on a log–log plot. Magnitudes are already logarithmic: $\log L=-0.4M+$ const.

steps.reveal: Over a factor $\sim100$ in $L$ (5 magnitudes) $\sigma$ grows by a factor $\sim3$: $\alpha\approx\log3/\log100\approx0.25$, i.e. $L\propto\sigma^4$ (Faber–Jackson).
steps.explain: Slope = change in $\log\sigma$ over change in $\log L$; reading two well separated points on the band is enough.

steps.reveal: Virial theorem $\sigma^2\propto M/R$ with a constant mass-to-light ratio and constant surface brightness ($L\propto R^2$) gives $L\propto\sigma^4$.
steps.explain: Virial: $\sigma^2\sim GM/R$. If $M\propto L$ and all ellipticals have the same surface brightness, $L\propto R^2$, then $\sigma^4\propto M^2/R^2\propto L$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 9.3: Maximum superluminal motion
enc.goal: A jet blob moves at $0.98c$. At what angle to the line of sight is the apparent superluminal motion largest, and what is the maximum apparent transverse velocity?

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1-\beta\cos\theta}=0\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\beta$.
steps.explain: Differentiate the quotient: numerator of the derivative $\cos\theta(1-\beta\cos\theta)-\sin\theta\cdot\beta\sin\theta=\cos\theta-\beta$; zero at $\cos\theta=\beta$.

steps.reveal: $\theta=\arccos0.98\approx11.5^\circ$; $v_{\rm app,max}=\beta\gamma c=0.98\times5.03\,c\approx4.92c$.
steps.explain: Insert: $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}=1/\gamma$ and $1-\beta^2=1/\gamma^2$, so $v_{\rm app}=v\frac{1/\gamma}{1/\gamma^2}=\beta\gamma c$.

steps.reveal: The blob almost catches up with its own light: emission times are compressed by $1-\beta\cos\theta$, so the projected motion looks faster than $c$ though nothing moves faster than light.
steps.explain: The blob moves almost toward us, so light emitted later has a shorter way to travel. The time between two observed positions is compressed, and the apparent speed (sideways distance / observed time) can exceed $c$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 9.4: Synchrotron electrons in a radio jet
enc.goal: With $B\sim10^{-10}$ T in jets, estimate $\gamma$ of electrons emitting synchrotron radio waves and their cooling time from (8.59). Compare with the travel time over a $1$ Mpc jet at $0.1c$. Must the electrons be re-accelerated in the jet?

steps.reveal: $\nu_g=2.8$ Hz, so $\gamma\approx\sqrt{10^9/\nu_g}\approx1.9\times10^{4}$.
steps.explain: An electron spirals around the field at the gyrofrequency; relativistic beaming concentrates its emission at $\sim\gamma^2$ times that. Invert for $\gamma$ at radio frequencies.

steps.reveal: $t=\dfrac{\gamma m_ec^2}{P}=\dfrac{m_ec}{\frac43\sigma_T\gamma U_B}\approx1.3\times10^{9}$ yr, with $U_B=4\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.
steps.explain: Cooling time = energy / power lost. Synchrotron power grows with $\gamma^2$, energy with $\gamma$, so faster electrons cool faster.

steps.reveal: $1\ \mathrm{Mpc}/0.1c\approx3.3\times10^{7}$ yr: shorter than the synchrotron cooling time.
steps.explain: Distance / speed, in years.

steps.reveal: Synchrotron losses alone would let nucleus-accelerated electrons reach the lobes. But inverse Compton scattering on the CMB acts like a field with $U_{\rm CMB}=4.2\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$ (10 times $U_B$), cutting the lifetime to $\approx1.1\times10^{8}$ yr; with stronger fields in the lobes and adiabatic losses, in-situ acceleration (shocks, hot spots) is in fact needed.
steps.explain: Compare the two times. Inverse Compton scattering off CMB photons acts like an extra magnetic field with energy density $U_{\rm CMB}$ and must be added to the losses.

enc.title: Choudhuri 9.5: Are galaxy clusters virialized?
enc.goal: Estimate the time a galaxy takes to cross a cluster of galaxies and the relaxation time. A cluster is clearly not relaxed, but the virial theorem only needs it to be virialized. Are typical clusters virialized?

steps.reveal: $T_{\rm cross}=R/v\approx9.8\times10^{8}$ yr, about $10^9$ yr.
steps.explain: Crossing time = size / typical speed; convert Mpc and km/s to s, then to years.

steps.reveal: $T_{\rm rel}\approx NT_{\rm cross}\approx9.8\times10^{11}$ yr, far longer than the age of the Universe: two-body encounters have not relaxed the cluster.
steps.explain: Relaxation (exchange of energy by individual encounters) takes about $N$ crossings (more precisely $N/(8\ln N)$, still enormous).

steps.reveal: The age ($\sim10^{10}$ yr) is about ten crossing times: enough for violent relaxation to bring the system into a steady state, so rich clusters are roughly virialized (supported by their smooth X-ray gas). Young, irregular clusters with substructure are not, and the virial mass there is uncertain.
steps.explain: Relaxed vs virialised: relaxed means individual galaxies have exchanged energy (thermalised); virialised only means the system as a whole is in a steady state, where the virial theorem $2K+U=0$ holds. Steady state needs only a few crossing times (violent relaxation).

keyPoints: virial equilibrium needs only a few crossing times

enc.title: Choudhuri 10.1: Density parameter independent of $h$
enc.goal: Distances from Hubble’s law scale as $h^{-1}$. If the mean density comes from virial masses of galaxy clusters, show that the density parameter is independent of the uncertainty in $H_0$.

steps.reveal: $\sigma$ is measured (redshifts): no $h$. $R=\theta d\propto h^{-1}$, so $M\propto h^{-1}$. The number of clusters per unit volume $\propto d^{-3}\propto h^3$.
steps.explain: Track every quantity: what is measured directly (angles, redshifts, velocity dispersions) carries no $h$; anything turned into a distance via Hubble's law, $d=cz/H_0$, carries $h^{-1}$.

steps.reveal: $\rho=n_{\rm cl}M\propto h^3h^{-1}=h^2$ (equivalently, $M/L\propto h$ and the luminosity density $\propto h$).
steps.explain: Mass density = number per volume × mass each: $h^3\cdot h^{-1}=h^2$.

steps.reveal: $\Omega=\rho/\rho_c\propto h^2/h^2$: independent of $h$. That is why $\Omega_{M,0}\approx0.3$ was robust while $H_0$ was still disputed.
steps.explain: The critical density also scales as $H_0^2\propto h^2$, so the ratio does not depend on $h$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 10.2: Age of the Universe when quasar light left
enc.goal: For quasars at $z=1$ and $z=4$, find the age of the Universe (as a fraction of today’s) when the light left, for $\Omega_{M,0}=1$. Estimate the errors if instead $\Omega_{M,0}=0.5$ or $1.5$ (matter only).

steps.explain: For matter only and flat space, $\dot a^2\propto1/a$, so $a\propto t^{2/3}$. Then $t\propto a^{3/2}=(1+z)^{-3/2}$ relative to today.

steps.reveal: Integrating numerically: $t/t_0=0.39$ and $0.106$, i.e. $10.2\%$ and $18.3\%$ larger than the EdS estimate.
steps.explain: Non-flat cases: no simple power law, so evaluate the integral numerically (or with the parametric cycloid solutions). Compare the fraction with the flat case.
Same for the closed model.

steps.reveal: The fraction depends only weakly on $\Omega$; the error grows with $z$ because the curvature term changes the early expansion history relative to today.
steps.explain: The ratio $t/t_0$ is insensitive to $\Omega$ because the early Universe is matter dominated in all cases; curvature only matters late.

enc.title: Choudhuri 10.3: Age against $\Omega_{M,0}$ (Fig. 10.6)
enc.goal: Assuming a matter-dominated Universe, calculate numerically the age for different $\Omega_{M,0}$ and reproduce Figure 10.6.

steps.reveal: Friedmann with $\rho\propto a^{-3}$ and curvature fixed by $\Omega_{M,0}$: $\dot a=H_0\sqrt{\Omega_{M,0}/a+1-\Omega_{M,0}}$, and $t_0=\int_0^1da/\dot a$.
steps.explain: Friedmann: $H^2=H_0^2(\Omega_{M,0}a^{-3}+\Omega_{k,0}a^{-2})$ with $\Omega_{k,0}=1-\Omega_{M,0}$. Multiply by $a^2$ for $\dot a^2$, take the root; time = $\int da/\dot a$.
Numerical integration for each $\Omega$; check the flat case $\int_0^1\sqrt a\,da=\frac23$.

steps.reveal: From $12.5$ Gyr ($\Omega=0.1$) down to $9.31$ Gyr ($\Omega=1$): younger than the oldest globular clusters for $\Omega=1$, the old "age problem" solved by $\Omega_\Lambda$.
steps.explain: Multiply by the Hubble time $1/H_0$. A denser Universe decelerated more, so it reached today's expansion rate in less time: it is younger.

enc.title: Choudhuri 10.4: Radiation-only universes
enc.goal: Suppose the Universe had only radiation. Solve the Friedmann equation for $k=0,+1,-1$ and sketch $a(t)$.
given: $\dot a^2=\dfrac{8\pi G}3\rho a^2-kc^2$, $\rho\propto a^{-4}$: $\dot a^2=\dfrac{C}{a^2}-kc^2$, $C=\dfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_0a_0^4$

steps.reveal: $a\dot a=\sqrt{C-kc^2a^2}\Rightarrow\dot u=2\sqrt{C-kc^2u}$.
steps.explain: Radiation density $\propto a^{-4}$ (number $\propto a^{-3}$, each photon's energy redshifts $\propto a^{-1}$). Multiplying $\dot a^2=C/a^2-kc^2$ by $a^2$ gives $(a\dot a)^2$, and $a\dot a=\frac12\frac{d}{dt}a^2$: hence $u=a^2$.

steps.reveal: $u=2\sqrt Ct$: $a=(2\sqrt C\,t)^{1/2}\propto t^{1/2}$.
steps.explain: $\dot u=2\sqrt C$: linear growth, $a\propto\sqrt t$.

steps.reveal: $k=+1$: $\sqrt{C-c^2u}=\sqrt C-c^2t$, so $a=\sqrt{2\sqrt Ct-c^2t^2}$: a half circle, maximum at $t=\sqrt C/c^2$, crunch at $2\sqrt C/c^2$. $k=-1$: $a=\sqrt{2\sqrt Ct+c^2t^2}$, approaching $a\approx ct$ (coasting).
steps.explain: Separate variables: $\frac{du}{2\sqrt{C-kc^2u}}=dt$ integrates to a square root, which you then square. Closed: grows, stops, recollapses. Open: eventually $a\approx ct$.

steps.reveal: All three start as $t^{1/2}$ at small $t$ (curvature is irrelevant early); they separate when $kc^2a^2\sim C$.
steps.explain: Near $t=0$ the radiation term $C/a^2$ dominates the constant curvature term: all models look the same early on.

enc.title: Choudhuri 10.5: Creation rate in the steady-state theory
enc.goal: In the steady-state theory the density stays constant through continuous creation of matter. Using (9.17) and (10.43), estimate how many hydrogen atoms must be created per year in $1\ \mathrm{km^3}$.
given: $\dot n=3Hn$ keeps $n$ constant while volumes grow as $a^3$

steps.reveal: A comoving volume grows as $a^3$: $\dot V/V=3H$. To keep $n=N/V$ constant, $\dot N=3HN$ per volume.
steps.explain: Expansion stretches every length by $a$, so volumes grow like $a^3$ and $\frac{\dot V}{V}=3\frac{\dot a}{a}=3H$. Keeping the density constant requires new particles at that rate.

steps.reveal: $n=\rho/m_H\approx1.65\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $H_0=2.3\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$; $3H_0n\times10^9\ \mathrm{m^3}\times1$ yr gives $\approx0.355$ atoms per $\mathrm{km^3}$ per year (about $1.18$ for the critical density).
steps.explain: Density from $\Omega$ and $h$, divided by the hydrogen mass gives atoms per m$^3$; multiply by $3H_0$, by $10^9$ m$^3$ and by one year in seconds.

steps.reveal: About one atom per cubic kilometre per year: far too little to test in a laboratory. The theory failed on other grounds (CMB, evolution of radio sources).
steps.explain: An undetectably small rate, so the idea could not be ruled out directly; the CMB did it.

keyPoints: untestable locally, ruled out by the CMB

enc.title: Choudhuri 11.1: Number and energy densities of relativistic bosons and fermions
enc.goal: (a) Using $\zeta(n)=\sum k^{-n}$ and $\dfrac1{e^x-1}=\sum_{k\ge1}e^{-kx}$, derive (11.9) for bosons from (11.7), and (11.10) from (11.8) using $\zeta(4)=\pi^4/90$. (b) With $I_n^\pm=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{x^ndx}{e^x\pm1}$ show $I_n^--I_n^+=2^{-n}I_n^-$ and derive the fermion results.

steps.reveal: $I_n^-=\sum_k\displaystyle\int x^ne^{-kx}dx=\sum_k\frac{n!}{k^{n+1}}=n!\,\zeta(n+1)$: $I_2^-=2\zeta(3)$, $I_3^-=6\zeta(4)=\pi^4/15$.
steps.explain: Expand the Bose factor as a geometric series in $e^{-x}$; each term integrates to a Gamma function, $\int x^ne^{-kx}dx=n!/k^{n+1}$, and the sum over $k$ is a zeta function.

steps.reveal: $n=\dfrac{g}{2\pi^2}\left(\dfrac{\kappa_BT}{\hbar c}\right)^32\zeta(3)=\dfrac{\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}g\left(\dfrac{\kappa_BT}{\hbar c}\right)^3$ (11.9); $\rho c^2=\dfrac{g}{2\pi^2}\dfrac{(\kappa_BT)^4}{(\hbar c)^3}\dfrac{\pi^4}{15}=\dfrac g2a_BT^4$ (11.10).
steps.explain: Substitute $x=pc/kT$ in (11.7) and (11.8) to pull out $T^3$ and $T^4$, then insert the integrals.

steps.prompt: (b) The difference of the two integrals.
steps.reveal: $\dfrac1{e^x-1}-\dfrac1{e^x+1}=\dfrac2{e^{2x}-1}$, so $I_n^--I_n^+=2\displaystyle\int\frac{x^ndx}{e^{2x}-1}=\frac{2}{2^{n+1}}I_n^-=2^{-n}I_n^-$.
steps.explain: Algebra with common denominators: $\frac{1}{e^x-1}-\frac{1}{e^x+1}=\frac{2}{e^{2x}-1}$. Substituting $y=2x$ in the last integral gives $2^{-(n+1)}$ times the Bose integral.

steps.reveal: $I_n^+=(1-2^{-n})I_n^-$: factor $\frac34$ for $n$ ($n=2$) and $\frac78$ for $\rho$ ($n=3$): $n_F=\frac34\dfrac{\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}g\left(\dfrac{\kappa_BT}{\hbar c}\right)^3$, $\rho_Fc^2=\frac78\dfrac g2a_BT^4$.
steps.explain: Fermions: $I^+=I^--2^{-n}I^-$. Pauli exclusion makes fermions slightly less numerous and energetic than bosons at the same $T$: the famous $\frac34$ and $\frac78$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 11.2: Helium if neutrons froze out at 0.4 MeV
enc.goal: If $n+\nu_e\leftrightarrow p+e^-$ had dropped below the expansion rate only at $T\approx0.4$ MeV, what would the helium abundance be?

steps.reveal: $n_n/n_p=e^{-1.29/0.4}\approx0.0398$ (instead of 0.20 at 0.8 MeV).
steps.explain: In equilibrium neutrons and protons follow Boltzmann with their mass difference; when the reactions stop, the ratio is frozen at the value at that temperature. A lower freeze-out temperature leaves fewer neutrons.

steps.reveal: $Y\approx\dfrac{2\times0.0398}{1+0.0398}\approx0.0765$, an upper bound; neutron decay before nucleosynthesis lowers it further.
steps.explain: All surviving neutrons end up in helium (2 n + 2 p): the helium mass fraction is twice the neutron fraction.

steps.reveal: $Y$ is exponentially sensitive to the freeze-out temperature, which is set by the weak rate versus $H$. The observed $Y\approx0.25$ therefore tests the weak interaction and the expansion rate (e.g. the number of neutrino species).
steps.explain: The ratio depends exponentially on $T_{\rm freeze}$, and $T_{\rm freeze}$ depends on how fast the Universe expanded (more neutrino species = faster expansion = earlier freeze-out = more helium).

enc.title: Choudhuri 11.3: Chemical potentials of electrons and positrons
enc.goal: Before $e^+e^-$ annihilation there were slightly more electrons than positrons. Show that their chemical potentials must then be non-zero, and explain how to calculate them.

steps.reveal: With $\mu=0$ the Fermi–Dirac distributions of $e^-$ and $e^+$ are identical, so $n_-=n_+$. An excess needs $\mu_->0$; the pair equilibrium with photons ($\mu_\gamma=0$) forces $\mu_+=-\mu_-$.
steps.explain: A chemical potential shifts the occupation numbers; with $\mu=0$ particles and antiparticles have identical distributions. Reactions in equilibrium conserve $\sum\mu$: photons have $\mu=0$, so $\mu_++\mu_-=0$.

steps.reveal: Charge neutrality: $n_--n_+=n_p\approx\eta n_\gamma$ with $\eta\sim6\times10^{-10}$.
steps.explain: The universe is electrically neutral: the excess of electrons must equal the number of protons, which is $\eta$ times the photon number.

steps.reveal: For $\mu\ll\kappa_BT$ the bracket is linear: $\dfrac{g}{6}\left(\dfrac{\kappa_BT}{\hbar c}\right)^3\dfrac{\mu}{\kappa_BT}=\eta\dfrac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}\left(\dfrac{\kappa_BT}{\hbar c}\right)^3$, so with $g=2$: $\dfrac{\mu}{\kappa_BT}=\dfrac{6\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}\eta\approx0.7\eta\sim10^{-9}$, tiny but non-zero, and constant while the gas stays relativistic.
steps.explain: For tiny $\mu$ keep only the linear term, then solve for $\mu/kT$. Both sides scale as $T^3$, so $\mu/kT$ stays constant as the Universe cools (while the electrons are relativistic).

enc.title: Choudhuri 11.4: Recombination temperature from the Saha equation
enc.goal: Estimate the gas pressure at $z\approx1100$, take hydrogen at that pressure, and use the Saha equation (2.29) to compute $x(T)$. At what temperature does $x$ change from near 0 to near 1?

steps.reveal: $T\approx3e+03$ K, $n\approx3.3\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $P=n\kappa_BT\approx1.4\times10^{-11}$ Pa: an excellent laboratory vacuum.
steps.explain: Scale today's baryon density by $(1+z)^3$ and today's CMB temperature by $(1+z)$, then ideal gas law.

steps.prompt: Saha at that pressure (as in Exercise 2.3).
steps.explain: Saha at fixed density (as in Ex. 2.3), now with a much lower density, so ionisation persists to lower temperature only because of the huge number of photons per atom.

steps.reveal: $x=1/2$ at $T\approx3.68e+03$ K, and the change from 0.1 to 0.9 happens within a few hundred K. Hydrogen recombines at $\sim3500$ K, not at $\chi/\kappa_B=1.6\times10^5$ K, because there are $\sim10^9$ photons per baryon: the Wien tail keeps ionizing until $\kappa_BT\approx\chi/40$.
steps.explain: Even at $kT\approx0.3$ eV, far below 13.6 eV, the rare high-energy photons in the Wien tail ($10^9$ photons per baryon) keep hydrogen ionised. Recombination happens only when even that tail is too weak.

enc.title: Choudhuri 11.6: Growth of a density perturbation, $\delta\propto t^{2/3}$
enc.goal: A spherical shell at $a(t)$ is perturbed to $a+l$. Show $\ddot l=\dfrac{2GM}{a^3}l=\dfrac{8\pi G}3\rho l$. With $\delta=\delta\rho/\rho=-3l/a$ and a marginally critical background, derive $\ddot\delta+\dfrac4{3t}\dot\delta-\dfrac2{3t^2}\delta=0$ and show that $\delta\propto t^{2/3}$ solves it.

steps.reveal: $\ddot a+\ddot l=-\dfrac{GM}{(a+l)^2}\approx-\dfrac{GM}{a^2}+\dfrac{2GM}{a^3}l$, so $\ddot l=\dfrac{2GM}{a^3}l=\dfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho\,l$.
steps.explain: A shell at radius $a$ feels only the mass $M$ inside it (Newton's shell theorem works for a uniform expanding ball). Displace it slightly to $a+l$ and Taylor-expand $1/(a+l)^2\approx\frac1{a^2}(1-\frac{2l}{a})$; the zeroth order is the background equation and cancels. Then $M=\frac43\pi\rho a^3$.

steps.reveal: $l=-a\delta/3$: $\ddot l=-\frac13(\ddot a\delta+2\dot a\dot\delta+a\ddot\delta)$. With $\ddot a/a=-\frac{4\pi G}3\rho$: $\ddot\delta+2\dfrac{\dot a}a\dot\delta-4\pi G\rho\,\delta=0$.
steps.explain: A shell pushed out by $l$ dilutes the density inside by $\delta=-3l/a$ (volume $\propto$ radius cubed). Express $l$ through $\delta$ and differentiate the product twice (product rule gives three terms); use the background equation $\ddot a=-\frac{4\pi G}{3}\rho a$ to replace $\ddot a$.

steps.reveal: $\dot a/a=\dfrac2{3t}$, $4\pi G\rho=\dfrac2{3t^2}$: $\ddot\delta+\dfrac4{3t}\dot\delta-\dfrac2{3t^2}\delta=0$.
steps.explain: For the critical (flat, matter-only) background $a\propto t^{2/3}$, so $\dot a/a=\frac{2}{3t}$ and the Friedmann equation fixes $\rho$ in terms of $t$.

steps.reveal: $\delta=t^s$: $s(s-1)+\frac43s-\frac23=0\Rightarrow s=\frac23$ or $s=-1$. The growing mode $\delta\propto t^{2/3}\propto a$: perturbations grow only like the scale factor, so from $\delta\sim10^{-5}$ at $z=1100$ they reach $\sim10^{-2}$ today without dark matter (structure-formation argument for dark matter).
steps.explain: Power-law ansatz $\delta=t^s$ turns the equation into a quadratic for $s$. The growing solution $t^{2/3}$ is proportional to $a$: perturbations grow only as fast as the Universe expands, a slow growth that baryons alone cannot achieve from the tiny CMB fluctuations; dark matter starts earlier.

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.1: Curvature of three 2D metrics
enc.goal: Work out the Christoffel symbols, Riemann and Ricci tensors and the scalar curvature for $ds^2=dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$, $ds^2=a^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$ and $ds^2=a^2(d\chi^2+\sinh^2\chi\,d\eta^2)$.

steps.reveal: $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-r$, $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=1/r$; $R^r{}_{\theta r\theta}=\partial_r\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}-\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}\Gamma^\theta_{\theta r}\ldots=-1+1=0$: flat, $R=0$ (only the coordinates are curved).
steps.explain: Recipe: read $g_{ik}$ off $ds^2$, compute Christoffels from derivatives of $g$, then curvature. For the plane in polar coordinates the Christoffels are not zero (the coordinate lines curve), but the curvature comes out zero: curved coordinates on a flat space.

steps.reveal: $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}=\cot\theta$; $R_{\theta\phi\theta\phi}=a^2\sin^2\theta$, $R_{\theta\theta}=1$, $R_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta$, $R=\dfrac2{a^2}$.
steps.explain: Only $g_{\phi\phi}=a^2\sin^2\theta$ depends on a coordinate, so only Christoffels involving $\partial_\theta g_{\phi\phi}$ survive. In 2D there is just one independent curvature component; the result $R=2/a^2$ is the same at every point, as a sphere must be.

steps.reveal: Same with $\sin\to\sinh$: $\Gamma^\chi_{\eta\eta}=-\sinh\chi\cosh\chi$, $\Gamma^\eta_{\chi\eta}=\coth\chi$; $R_{\chi\chi}=-1$, $R_{\eta\eta}=-\sinh^2\chi$, $R=-\dfrac2{a^2}$.
steps.explain: Replace $\sin\to\sinh$: derivatives differ by a sign ($\sinh''=+\sinh$ while $\sin''=-\sin$), which flips the sign of the curvature.

steps.reveal: Constant curvature $K=R/2=+1/a^2,0,-1/a^2$: the 2D analogues of closed, flat and open Robertson–Walker spaces (the sign convention of the book fixes the sign of $R$).
steps.explain: Gaussian curvature $K=R/2$: positive (sphere, triangles add to more than $180^\circ$), zero (plane), negative (saddle). These are the 2D versions of closed, flat and open universes.

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.2: Covariant derivatives do not commute
enc.goal: Show that two covariant derivatives in general do not commute, and for a contravariant vector $\left(\dfrac{D}{Dx^k}\dfrac{D}{Dx^l}-\dfrac{D}{Dx^l}\dfrac{D}{Dx^k}\right)A^i=-R^i{}_{mlk}A^m$ (book sign convention).

steps.reveal: $A^i{}_{;l;k}=\partial_k(\partial_lA^i+\Gamma^i_{ml}A^m)+\Gamma^i_{nk}(\partial_lA^n+\Gamma^n_{ml}A^m)-\Gamma^n_{lk}A^i{}_{;n}$.
steps.explain: $A^i{}_{;l}$ is a tensor with one upper and one lower index, so the second covariant derivative needs the formula for such a tensor: one $+\Gamma$ for the upper index, one $-\Gamma$ for the lower one.

steps.reveal: $\partial_k\partial_lA^i$ and $\Gamma^n_{lk}A^i{}_{;n}$ are symmetric and cancel; the terms $\Gamma\,\partial A$ cancel crosswise. What is left multiplies $A^m$: $\left(\partial_k\Gamma^i_{ml}-\partial_l\Gamma^i_{mk}+\Gamma^i_{nk}\Gamma^n_{ml}-\Gamma^i_{nl}\Gamma^n_{mk}\right)A^m$.
steps.explain: Antisymmetrise: anything symmetric in $k$ and $l$ cancels in the difference: ordinary second derivatives commute, and $\Gamma^n_{lk}$ is symmetric. The terms with $\partial A$ cancel between the two orders. Only terms with $A$ itself (no derivative) survive.

steps.reveal: With the book’s definition (12.37), $R^i{}_{mlk}=\partial_l\Gamma^i_{mk}-\partial_k\Gamma^i_{ml}+\Gamma^n_{mk}\Gamma^i_{nl}-\Gamma^n_{ml}\Gamma^i_{nk}$, the bracket is exactly $-R^i{}_{mlk}$. Since $\frac{D}{Dx^k}\frac{D}{Dx^l}A^i=A^i{}_{;l;k}$, this is the stated result. Derivatives commute only where the curvature vanishes.
steps.explain: Compare the leftover coefficient with the book's definition of the Riemann tensor; it matches up to a sign. Interpretation: transporting a vector around a small loop changes it exactly when space is curved.

keyPoints: covariant derivative of a mixed tensor
Riemann tensor emerges, sign by convention

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.3: Symmetries of $R_{iklm}$ and the contracted Bianchi step
enc.goal: From (12.37) build $R_{iklm}=g_{in}R^n{}_{klm}$, show $R_{iklm}=\frac12(\partial_k\partial_lg_{im}+\partial_i\partial_mg_{kl}-\partial_k\partial_mg_{il}-\partial_i\partial_lg_{km})+g_{np}(\Gamma^n_{kl}\Gamma^p_{im}-\Gamma^n_{km}\Gamma^p_{il})$, deduce $R_{iklm}=-R_{kilm}=-R_{ikml}=R_{lmik}$, and prove $g^{im}R^n{}_{ilm}=R^n{}_l$ (needed for $\nabla_kG^{ik}=0$).

steps.reveal: $g_{in}\partial_k\Gamma^n_{lm}=\partial_k\Gamma_{i,lm}-\Gamma^n_{lm}\partial_kg_{in}$; the second derivatives of $g$ come from $\partial\Gamma_{i,lm}=\frac12\partial(\partial g+\partial g-\partial g)$, the rest combine into the quadratic $\Gamma\Gamma$ terms.
steps.explain: Lowering the index of $\partial\Gamma$ produces a correction from $\partial g$; this is where the $\Gamma\Gamma$ terms get reshuffled. The second derivatives of $g$ come from differentiating the definition of the lowered Christoffel symbol.

steps.reveal: Read them off: swapping $i\leftrightarrow k$ or $l\leftrightarrow m$ flips the sign of both the derivative and $\Gamma\Gamma$ parts; swapping the pairs $(ik)\leftrightarrow(lm)$ leaves them unchanged (check in a locally geodesic frame where $\Gamma=0$).
steps.explain: Easiest in a locally flat (geodesic) frame where all $\Gamma=0$ at the point: only the four $\partial\partial g$ terms remain, and the symmetries can be read off by swapping indices. Since they are tensor equations, they hold in every frame.

steps.reveal: $g^{im}R^n{}_{ilm}=g^{im}g^{nk}R_{kilm}$. Pair symmetry and then both antisymmetries: $R_{kilm}=R_{lmki}=-R_{mlki}=R_{mlik}$. Contracting the first and third index with $g^{im}$ gives $g^{im}R_{mlik}=R^i{}_{lik}=R_{lk}$ by (12.41), and $R_{lk}=R_{kl}$. Hence $g^{im}R^n{}_{ilm}=g^{nk}R_{kl}=R^n{}_l$.
steps.explain: Use the symmetries to move the contracted indices into the position where the contraction defines the Ricci tensor, then use $R_{lk}=R_{kl}$.

keyPoints: lowering the index of the Riemann tensor

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.4: Geodesic deviation
enc.goal: For two neighbouring geodesics $x^i(s)$ and $x^i(s)+\delta x^i(s)$ show $\dfrac{D^2}{Ds^2}\delta x^i=-R^i{}_{klm}\delta x^l\dfrac{dx^k}{ds}\dfrac{dx^m}{ds}$ (book sign convention).

steps.prompt: Subtract the geodesic equations to first order.
steps.reveal: $\delta\ddot x^i+\partial_m\Gamma^i_{kl}\delta x^m\dot x^k\dot x^l+2\Gamma^i_{kl}\dot x^k\delta\dot x^l=0$.
steps.explain: Write the geodesic equation for both curves and subtract; keep only terms linear in $\delta x$. The Christoffel at the shifted point is Taylor-expanded: $\Gamma(x+\delta x)\approx\Gamma(x)+\partial_m\Gamma\,\delta x^m$.

steps.prompt: Rewrite with covariant derivatives along the curve.
steps.reveal: $\dfrac{D\delta x^i}{Ds}=\delta\dot x^i+\Gamma^i_{kl}\dot x^k\delta x^l$; differentiate again and use the geodesic equation to remove $\ddot x$.
steps.explain: $\delta\ddot x$ is not a tensor; the covariant derivative along the curve is. Express $\delta\ddot x$ through $D^2\delta x/Ds^2$ plus correction terms.

steps.reveal: All terms combine into $\left(\partial_l\Gamma^i_{km}-\partial_m\Gamma^i_{kl}+\Gamma\Gamma-\Gamma\Gamma\right)\dot x^k\dot x^m\delta x^l$, the Riemann tensor: the stated equation. Physics: tidal acceleration between free particles; in Newtonian terms $\ddot{\delta x}_i=-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi\,\delta x_j$.
steps.explain: After cancellations the coefficient of $\delta x\,\dot x\dot x$ is the Riemann tensor. Meaning: neighbouring free particles accelerate relative to each other only if spacetime is curved; this relative acceleration is the tidal force.

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.5: Great circles are geodesics, other latitude circles are not
enc.goal: Prove that the equator of a sphere is a geodesic, but any other circle of constant latitude is not.

steps.reveal: $\ddot\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\phi^2=0$.
steps.explain: The $\theta$-component of the geodesic equation with the sphere's Christoffels.

steps.reveal: Then $\ddot\theta=0$, so we need $\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0\dot\phi^2=0$: only $\theta_0=\pi/2$ works (the poles are trivial).
steps.explain: A latitude circle has $\theta$ constant, so $\ddot\theta=0$, and the equation then demands $\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0=0$: only the equator.

steps.reveal: $\ddot\phi+2\cot\theta\dot\theta\dot\phi=0$ holds for constant $\theta$ and constant $\dot\phi$. So the equator is a geodesic; a latitude circle needs a force pulling towards the pole axis: an airplane flying "due east" at $60^\circ$ N is constantly turning.
steps.explain: The $\phi$ equation is fine for any constant $\theta$; it is the $\theta$ equation that fails. Away from the equator, following a circle of latitude requires constant steering.

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.6: Metric of a rotating frame
enc.goal: With $ds^2=-c^2dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$ and the rotating coordinates $t'=t$, $z'=z$, $x'=x\cos\Omega t+y\sin\Omega t$, $y'=-x\sin\Omega t+y\cos\Omega t$, find $g_{ik}$ and $g^{ik}$ in the rotating frame and verify $g^{ik}g_{km}=\delta^i_m$.

steps.reveal: $dx=\cos\Omega t\,dx'-\sin\Omega t\,dy'-\Omega y\,dt$, $dy=\sin\Omega t\,dx'+\cos\Omega t\,dy'+\Omega x\,dt$ ($x,y$ expressed through $x',y'$). Then $dx^2+dy^2=dx'^2+dy'^2+2\Omega(x'dy'-y'dx')dt+\Omega^2(x'^2+y'^2)dt^2$.
steps.explain: Invert the rotation to get $x,y$ in terms of $x',y'$, then differentiate, remembering that $t$ appears in the angles: $\frac{d}{dt}\cos\Omega t=-\Omega\sin\Omega t$ produces the $dt$ terms.

steps.reveal: $ds^2=-\left(c^2-\Omega^2(x'^2+y'^2)\right)dt^2+2\Omega x'dy'dt-2\Omega y'dx'dt+dx'^2+dy'^2+dz'^2$: $g_{tt}=-(c^2-\Omega^2\varrho^2)$, $g_{tx}=-\Omega y'$, $g_{ty}=\Omega x'$, $g_{xx}=g_{yy}=g_{zz}=1$.
steps.explain: Insert into the flat metric and collect coefficients of $dt^2$, $dt\,dx'$, $dt\,dy'$, …: these are the metric components. Rotation produces off-diagonal $dt\,dx$ terms.

steps.reveal: $g^{tt}=-1/c^2$, $g^{tx}=-\Omega y'/c^2$, $g^{ty}=\Omega x'/c^2$, $g^{xx}=1-\Omega^2y'^2/c^2$, $g^{yy}=1-\Omega^2x'^2/c^2$, $g^{xy}=\Omega^2x'y'/c^2$, $g^{zz}=1$. Multiplying out $g^{ik}g_{km}$ gives $\delta^i_m$ (e.g. $g^{tt}g_{tt}+g^{tx}g_{xt}+g^{ty}g_{yt}=\frac{c^2-\Omega^2\varrho^2}{c^2}+\frac{\Omega^2y^2}{c^2}+\frac{\Omega^2x^2}{c^2}=1$).
steps.explain: For the inverse, verify by multiplication ($g^{ik}g_{km}=\delta^i_m$) rather than inverting a $4\times4$ matrix from scratch.

steps.reveal: $g_{tt}$ vanishes at $\varrho=c/\Omega$ (light cylinder); the off-diagonal $g_{ti}$ produce the Coriolis force. The space is still flat (all Riemann components zero).
steps.explain: At $\varrho=c/\Omega$ a point fixed in the rotating frame would move at $c$: the frame cannot be realised by observers beyond that. The spacetime is still Minkowski, just in rotating coordinates.

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.7: Einstein tensor of the weak-field metric
enc.goal: For $ds^2=-\left(1+\dfrac{2\Phi}{c^2}\right)c^2dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$ (non-relativistic particle in a weak field), calculate $G_{xx}$ and check the $xx$ component of Einstein’s equation. If it fails, how do you account for it?
given: to first order in $\Phi$; static field
$T_{ik}$ of dust: only $T_{tt}=\rho c^2$ (in these units)

steps.reveal: With $x^0=ct$ and $h_{00}=-2\Phi/c^2$ the linearised Ricci tensor gives $R_{00}=\nabla^2\Phi/c^2$, $R_{ij}=-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi/c^2$, so $R=-R_{00}+R_{ii}=-2\nabla^2\Phi/c^2$ (signature $-+++$).
steps.explain: For a small perturbation of flat spacetime the Ricci tensor is linear in second derivatives of $h$. Static field: time derivatives vanish, and only $h_{00}$ is non-zero here.

steps.reveal: $G_{xx}=R_{xx}-\frac12R=\dfrac{1}{c^2}\left(\nabla^2\Phi-\partial_x^2\Phi\right)=\dfrac{1}{c^2}(\partial_y^2+\partial_z^2)\Phi\neq0$ inside matter.
steps.explain: $G_{xx}=R_{xx}-\frac12g_{xx}R$ with $g_{xx}=1$.

steps.reveal: $T_{xx}=P\approx0$ for slow matter, but $G_{xx}\ne0$: the equation fails.
steps.explain: Dust at rest has no pressure, so $T_{xx}\approx0$; but $G_{xx}$ is not zero where $\nabla^2\Phi\neq0$.

steps.reveal: The metric is incomplete: at the same order the spatial part also changes, $g_{ij}=(1-2\Phi/c^2)\delta_{ij}$. With it $G_{ij}=0$ and only the $tt$ equation survives, giving $\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho$. The given metric reproduces particle motion (only $g_{tt}$ matters for slow particles), but not light bending, which needs the spatial part too (factor 2 in the deflection).
steps.explain: The ansatz was too simple: at the same order in $\Phi/c^2$ the spatial metric must change too. Slow particles barely feel $g_{ij}$, so Newtonian motion came out right, but light moves through space as fast as through time and feels both: hence twice the Newtonian bending.

keyPoints: missing spatial part of the metric

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.1: Lengths, areas and volumes in a curved static metric
enc.goal: For $ds^2=-(1-Ar^2)dt^2+(1-Ar^2)^{\pm1}dr^2+r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta d\phi^2)$ calculate (a) the proper radial distance from $r=0$ to $r=R$, (b) the area of the sphere $r=R$, (c) the 3-volume inside it, (d) the 4-volume of the tube between two $t=$ const surfaces separated by $T$.
given: Note: Our text copy shows $g_{rr}=1-Ar^2$; the superscript $-1$ may have been lost. Both versions are solved: use the one printed in your book.

steps.reveal: $\sqrt{g_{\theta\theta}g_{\phi\phi}}=r^2\sin\theta$: $4\pi R^2$ in both cases ($r$ is defined by the area).
steps.explain: On a sphere $r=R$, $t=$ const, only $d\theta$ and $d\phi$ vary; the area element is $\sqrt{g_{\theta\theta}g_{\phi\phi}}\,d\theta\,d\phi$. Since those components are $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\theta$, the area is the flat one: this is how $r$ is defined.

steps.reveal: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^R\frac{dr}{\sqrt{1-Ar^2}}=\frac{\arcsin(\sqrt AR)}{\sqrt A}$ ($>R$). (c) $4\pi\displaystyle\int_0^R\frac{r^2dr}{\sqrt{1-Ar^2}}=\frac{2\pi}{A^{3/2}}\left[\arcsin(\sqrt AR)-\sqrt AR\sqrt{1-AR^2}\right]$. (d) $\sqrt{-g}=r^2\sin\theta$: $\frac43\pi R^3T$.
steps.explain: Radial proper length integrates $\sqrt{g_{rr}}\,dr$. With $g_{rr}=(1-Ar^2)^{-1}$ the integral is an arcsine (substitute $r=\sin u/\sqrt A$). Volumes use $\sqrt{g_{rr}}r^2$; the 4-volume uses $\sqrt{-g}$, where $g_{tt}g_{rr}=-1$ simplifies.

steps.reveal: (a) $\frac12\left[R\sqrt{1-AR^2}+\frac{\arcsin(\sqrt AR)}{\sqrt A}\right]$ ($<R$). (c) $4\pi\int_0^Rr^2\sqrt{1-Ar^2}dr$. (d) $\sqrt{-g}=(1-Ar^2)r^2\sin\theta$: $4\pi T\left(\frac{R^3}3-\frac{AR^5}5\right)$.
steps.explain: Same integrals with $\sqrt{1-Ar^2}$ in the numerator; the volume is a standard integral as well.

steps.reveal: All reduce to the flat results $R$, $4\pi R^2$, $\frac43\pi R^3$, $\frac43\pi R^3T$.
steps.explain: Setting $A=0$ is the flat check; all results should reduce to Euclidean geometry.

keyPoints: area is $4\pi R^2$ by definition of $r$

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.2: Schwarzschild solves the vacuum equations
enc.goal: Show that the Schwarzschild metric (13.13) satisfies all components of Einstein’s vacuum equation for $r\neq0$.

steps.reveal: $\Gamma^t_{tr}=\alpha'$, $\Gamma^r_{tt}=c^2\alpha'e^{2(\alpha-\beta)}$, $\Gamma^r_{rr}=\beta'$, $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-re^{-2\beta}$, $\Gamma^r_{\phi\phi}=-re^{-2\beta}\sin^2\theta$, $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=\Gamma^\phi_{r\phi}=1/r$, $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}=\cot\theta$.
steps.explain: Write the general static spherical metric with two unknown functions; its Christoffels follow from derivatives of $e^{2\alpha}$, $e^{2\beta}$ and $r^2$.

steps.reveal: $R_{tt}\propto\alpha''+\alpha'^2-\alpha'\beta'+\frac2r\alpha'$, $R_{rr}=-\alpha''-\alpha'^2+\alpha'\beta'+\frac2r\beta'$, $R_{\theta\theta}=1-e^{-2\beta}\left[1+r(\alpha'-\beta')\right]$, $R_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta R_{\theta\theta}$.
steps.explain: Ricci components from the Christoffels (long but mechanical). Vacuum means all must vanish.

steps.reveal: $e^{2(\beta-\alpha)}R_{tt}/c^2+R_{rr}=\frac2r(\alpha'+\beta')=0\Rightarrow\alpha=-\beta$ (with flat infinity). Then $R_{\theta\theta}=0$ gives $(re^{2\alpha})'=1$, $e^{2\alpha}=1-\dfrac{2GM}{c^2r}$: exactly (13.13); with it $R_{tt}=R_{rr}=0$ too.
steps.explain: The clever combination: adding the $tt$ and $rr$ equations with the right weights cancels the second derivatives and leaves $\alpha'+\beta'=0$. Then the $\theta\theta$ equation becomes a first-order equation for $e^{2\alpha}$, solved by $1-\frac{2GM}{c^2r}$, with $M$ the integration constant (matched to Newton far away).

keyPoints: Christoffel symbols of the static spherical metric

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.3: Newtonian orbits from the Schwarzschild orbit equation
enc.goal: Neglecting the relativistic term, substitute $u_0=\frac1p(1+\epsilon\cos\phi)$ (13.32) into (13.28), $l^2\left(\frac{du}{d\phi}\right)^2=e^2-1-2V_{\rm eff}(u)$, to show $\epsilon=\sqrt{1+\dfrac{(e^2-1)l^2}{M^2}}$, the condition for an ellipse, $a=\dfrac{l^2}{M(1-\epsilon^2)}$ and $\dfrac{e^2-1}2=-\dfrac M{2a}$ ($G=c=1$). Meaning of the last result?

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{du}{d\phi}=-\dfrac\epsilon p\sin\phi$: $\dfrac{l^2\epsilon^2}{p^2}\sin^2\phi=e^2-1+\dfrac{2M}p(1+\epsilon\cos\phi)-\dfrac{l^2}{p^2}(1+\epsilon\cos\phi)^2$.
steps.explain: Without the GR term this is the Newtonian orbit equation. Try the conic section $u=\frac1p(1+\epsilon\cos\phi)$ and differentiate.

steps.reveal: $\cos\phi$ terms: $\dfrac{2M\epsilon}p=\dfrac{2l^2\epsilon}{p^2}\Rightarrow p=\dfrac{l^2}M$. Constant terms: $\dfrac{l^2\epsilon^2}{p^2}=e^2-1+\dfrac{2M}p-\dfrac{l^2}{p^2}\Rightarrow\epsilon^2=1+\dfrac{(e^2-1)l^2}{M^2}$.
steps.explain: The equation must hold for every $\phi$, so coefficients of $\cos\phi$, $\cos^2\phi$ and constants must match separately ($\sin^2=1-\cos^2$). That gives $p$ and $\epsilon$.

steps.reveal: $\epsilon<1\Leftrightarrow e^2<1$ (bound). Then $r_{\min,\max}=p/(1\pm\epsilon)$, $a=\dfrac{p}{1-\epsilon^2}=\dfrac{l^2}{M(1-\epsilon^2)}$, and $\dfrac{e^2-1}{2}=\dfrac{M^2(\epsilon^2-1)}{2l^2}=-\dfrac M{2a}$.
steps.explain: An ellipse has $\epsilon<1$; its closest and farthest distances $p/(1\pm\epsilon)$ average to the semi-major axis.

steps.reveal: $e$ is the conserved energy per unit rest energy, so $\frac{e^2-1}2\approx e-1$ is the Newtonian energy per unit mass: $E=-\dfrac{GM}{2a}$, the Kepler result that the energy depends only on the semimajor axis.
steps.explain: $e$ is the energy per rest energy; for slow orbits $e\approx1+E/mc^2$, so $\frac{e^2-1}{2}\approx E/mc^2$, the Newtonian energy: Kepler's $-GM/2a$ recovered.

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.4: Perihelion of Mercury and light bending by the Sun
enc.goal: (a) Calculate the perihelion precession of Mercury in arcseconds per century ($a=5.79\times10^7$ km, $\epsilon=0.206$, $P=88.0$ d). (b) Evaluate the maximum deflection of light by the Sun.

steps.reveal: $\Delta\phi=\dfrac{6\pi\times1.33\times10^{20}}{9\times10^{16}\times5.79\times10^{10}\times(1-0.206^2)}\approx5\times10^{-7}$ rad.
steps.explain: Insert $GM_\odot=1.33\times10^{20}$ m$^3$/s$^2$, $c^2$, $a$ in m and the eccentricity factor.

steps.reveal: $415$ orbits per century: $\approx42.9^{\prime\prime}$, the famous $43^{\prime\prime}$ unexplained by Newtonian perturbations.
steps.explain: Orbits per century: $36525/88$. Convert radians to arcseconds ($\times206265$).

steps.prompt: Light deflection at the solar limb.
steps.reveal: $\delta=\dfrac{4GM_\odot}{c^2R_\odot}\approx1.75^{\prime\prime}$, twice the "Newtonian" value; confirmed in the 1919 eclipse.
steps.explain: Grazing ray: $R=R_\odot$. Twice the Newtonian value because space is curved too (see Ex. 12.7).

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.5: Escape cone of light near a black hole
enc.goal: Light is emitted at $r_i$ with $2M<r_i<3M$ ($G=c=1$) at angle $\alpha$ to the radial direction. Show it escapes only if $\sin\alpha<\dfrac{3\sqrt3M}{r_i}\left(1-\dfrac{2M}{r_i}\right)^{1/2}$, so at $r=2M$ only radial light escapes.
given: photon orbit: $\left(\dfrac{du}{d\phi}\right)^2=\dfrac1{b^2}-u^2(1-2Mu)$, maximum of $u^2(1-2Mu)$ at $r=3M$ equals $\dfrac1{27M^2}$

steps.prompt: Angle measured by a static observer.
steps.reveal: Proper radial and tangential distances: $d\ell_r=\dfrac{dr}{\sqrt{1-2M/r}}$, $d\ell_\phi=r\,d\phi$, so $\tan\alpha=\left(1-\dfrac{2M}{r_i}\right)^{1/2}r_i\left(\dfrac{d\phi}{dr}\right)_i$ (the hint).
steps.explain: A local observer measures angles with proper distances, not coordinate ones. Near a black hole radial proper distance is stretched by $1/\sqrt{1-2M/r}$, so the measured angle differs from the coordinate one.

steps.reveal: The photon orbit gives $\left(\dfrac{dr}{d\phi}\right)^2=r^4\left[\dfrac1{b^2}-\dfrac1{r^2}\left(1-\dfrac{2M}r\right)\right]$. Then $\tan^2\alpha=\dfrac{1-2M/r_i}{r_i^2/b^2-(1-2M/r_i)}$ and $\sin^2\alpha=\dfrac{\tan^2\alpha}{1+\tan^2\alpha}=\dfrac{b^2}{r_i^2}\left(1-\dfrac{2M}{r_i}\right)$, i.e. $\dfrac1{b^2}=\dfrac{1-2M/r_i}{r_i^2\sin^2\alpha}$.
steps.explain: Express $dr/d\phi$ via the photon orbit equation in terms of the impact parameter $b$; then $\sin\alpha$ simplifies neatly.

steps.reveal: Emitted inside the photon sphere ($r_i<3M$) moving outward, the photon escapes only if it passes over the barrier: $\dfrac1{b^2}>\dfrac1{27M^2}$, i.e. $\sin^2\alpha<\dfrac{27M^2}{r_i^2}\left(1-\dfrac{2M}{r_i}\right)$: the stated cone.
steps.explain: Inside $3M$ the effective potential for light has a maximum at $3M$; an outgoing photon escapes only if its "energy" $1/b^2$ exceeds that maximum $1/27M^2$. Translate into a condition on $\alpha$.

steps.reveal: At $r_i\to2M$ the right side $\to0$: only exactly radial light escapes; the escape cone closes.
steps.explain: At the horizon the factor $1-2M/r$ is 0: the escape cone shrinks to a line. Just inside, nothing escapes.

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.6: Static weak field is not a transverse-traceless wave
enc.goal: Far from a spherical star the field is weak. (a) Find $h_{ik}$ in a suitable gauge. (b) Show that no gauge transformation brings it to the transverse-traceless form (13.84).
given: gauge freedom $h_{ik}\to h_{ik}-\partial_i\xi_k-\partial_k\xi_i$; Riemann tensor is gauge invariant

steps.reveal: $h_{tt}=\dfrac{2GM}{c^2r}$, $h_{ij}=\dfrac{2GM}{c^2r}\delta_{ij}$, $h_{ti}=0$ (from linearising Schwarzschild in isotropic coordinates); trace-reversed $\bar h_{tt}=4GM/c^2r$, others zero.
steps.explain: Far away Schwarzschild is weak; expanded to first order in $M/r$ (in isotropic coordinates) all diagonal components get $\frac{2GM}{c^2r}$. This is the Newtonian potential in GR clothing.

steps.reveal: A TT field has only $h_{xx}=-h_{yy}$, $h_{xy}$, depending on $ct-x^3$: it has no $tt$ component and its Riemann tensor $R_{titj}$ is transverse and traceless.
steps.explain: A TT wave only has spatial, transverse, traceless parts and oscillates as it propagates.

steps.reveal: The static field has $R_{titj}=\partial_i\partial_j\Phi/c^2$ with $\Phi=-GM/r$, whose trace $\nabla^2\Phi/c^2$ vanishes outside the star but which is not transverse (it has components along the radial direction) and does not oscillate. Since the Riemann tensor cannot be changed by gauge, no gauge makes $h$ TT: TT form is only possible for radiation, which obeys the vacuum wave equation with $\omega\neq0$.
steps.explain: Gauge-invariant test: the Riemann tensor does not change under coordinate changes. Compute it for the static field: it is not transverse and not oscillating, so no choice of gauge can make the field look like a wave.

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.7: No memory to linear order
enc.goal: A gravitational wave source emits for a finite time. A distant observer watches two free particles initially at rest. Show that after the wave has passed they are back at their original positions and at rest relative to each other (to linear order).
given: in TT gauge free particles stay at fixed coordinates; proper separation $L(t)=L_0\left(1+\frac12h_{ij}n^in^j\right)$

steps.prompt: Coordinates of free particles in TT gauge.
steps.reveal: The geodesic equation gives $\ddot x^i=-\Gamma^i_{tt}c^2=0$ in TT gauge (no $h_{tt}$, $h_{ti}$): they stay at fixed coordinates.
steps.explain: In TT gauge the relevant Christoffel $\Gamma^i_{tt}$ vanishes, so particles at rest stay at constant coordinates; the coordinates themselves "ride" the wave.

steps.reveal: $L(t)=L_0+\frac12h_{ij}(t)n^in^jL_0$: it oscillates while the wave passes.
steps.explain: Physical distance uses the metric: $\sqrt{(\delta_{ij}+h_{ij})dx^idx^j}\approx L_0(1+\frac12h_{ij}n^in^j)$. That is what a detector measures.

steps.reveal: For a finite wave train $h_{ij}\to0$ again (linear theory, no static part), so $L\to L_0$ and $\dot L=\frac12\dot h_{ij}n^in^jL_0\to0$: same positions, relative rest. (A permanent offset, the nonlinear "memory effect", appears only at higher order.)
steps.explain: Once the wave has passed, $h=0$ again, so the distance returns to $L_0$ and its rate of change to zero.

keyPoints: free particles at fixed TT coordinates

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.1: Scalar curvature of the 3-sphere and 3-hyperboloid
enc.goal: Find the scalar curvature of $ds^2=a^2[d\chi^2+\sin^2\chi(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)]$ and of the same metric with $\sinh\chi$.

steps.reveal: $\Gamma^\chi_{\theta\theta}=-\sin\chi\cos\chi$, $\Gamma^\chi_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\chi\cos\chi\sin^2\theta$, $\Gamma^\theta_{\chi\theta}=\Gamma^\phi_{\chi\phi}=\cot\chi$, $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}=\cot\theta$.
steps.explain: The 3-sphere metric in hyperspherical angles: only $\sin^2\chi$ and $\sin^2\theta$ depend on coordinates, giving these Christoffels.

steps.reveal: $R_{\chi\chi}=2$, $R_{\theta\theta}=2\sin^2\chi$, $R_{\phi\phi}=2\sin^2\chi\sin^2\theta$, i.e. $R_{ij}=\dfrac2{a^2}g_{ij}$.
steps.explain: Contract the Riemann tensor to Ricci. The result is proportional to the metric: maximally symmetric space, the same in every direction.

steps.reveal: $R=g^{ij}R_{ij}=\dfrac{6}{a^2}$ for the 3-sphere, $-\dfrac6{a^2}$ for the hyperbolic space ($\sin\to\sinh$ flips the sign of $K$).
steps.explain: Trace with $g^{ij}$ (3 dimensions): $R=3\cdot\frac{2}{a^2}$. $\sinh$ flips the sign.

steps.reveal: These are the spatial sections of the closed and open Robertson–Walker metrics with curvature $k/a^2$.
steps.explain: The spatial slices of the closed and open Robertson–Walker universes are exactly these spaces.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.2: Ricci tensor of the Robertson–Walker metric
enc.goal: Calculate all components of $R_{ik}$ for the Robertson–Walker metric and verify (14.2): $R_{tt}=-3\dfrac{\ddot a}a$, $R_{\alpha\beta}=\left(\dfrac{\ddot a}a+2\dfrac{\dot a^2}{a^2}+2\dfrac{kc^2}{a^2}\right)\dfrac{g_{\alpha\beta}}{c^2}$.

steps.reveal: $\Gamma^t_{\alpha\beta}=\dfrac{a\dot a}{c^2}\gamma_{\alpha\beta}$, $\Gamma^\alpha_{t\beta}=\dfrac{\dot a}a\delta^\alpha_\beta$, plus the purely spatial $\Gamma^\alpha_{\beta\gamma}$ of $\gamma$.
steps.explain: Time appears only through $a(t)$ in the spatial part, so the new Christoffels all contain $\dot a$.

steps.reveal: $R_{tt}=-\partial_t\Gamma^\alpha_{t\alpha}-\Gamma^\alpha_{t\beta}\Gamma^\beta_{t\alpha}=-3\dfrac{d}{dt}\dfrac{\dot a}a-3\dfrac{\dot a^2}{a^2}=-3\dfrac{\ddot a}a$.
steps.explain: Use the Ricci formula with these Christoffels. $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\dot a}{a}=\frac{\ddot a}{a}-\frac{\dot a^2}{a^2}$; the $\dot a^2$ terms cancel.

steps.reveal: Time-derivative terms give $\dfrac{1}{c^2}(a\ddot a+2\dot a^2)\gamma_{\alpha\beta}$, the spatial curvature adds $2k\gamma_{\alpha\beta}$ (from Exercise 14.1); with $g_{\alpha\beta}=a^2\gamma_{\alpha\beta}$ that is (14.2).
steps.explain: Spatial components: time-derivative pieces plus the curvature of the spatial slices themselves (Ex. 14.1).

steps.reveal: With $T_{ik}$ of a perfect fluid, the $tt$ and $\alpha\beta$ components of Einstein’s equation give the Friedmann and acceleration equations.
steps.explain: Inserting into Einstein's equations with a perfect fluid gives the two Friedmann equations.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.3: Instability of Einstein’s static universe
enc.goal: With a cosmological constant and $P=0$, let $a_0$ be the static solution. If $a$ is suddenly changed to $a_0+a_1$, show that $a_1$ grows exponentially.
given: $\ddot a=-\dfrac{4\pi G}3\rho a+\dfrac{\Lambda c^2}3a$, $\rho a^3=$ const

steps.reveal: $\ddot a=0\Rightarrow\Lambda c^2=4\pi G\rho_0$.
steps.explain: Static: $\ddot a=0$, so the attraction of matter balances the repulsion of $\Lambda$.

steps.reveal: Write $\rho a=\rho_0a_0^3/a^2$: $\ddot a_1=\left[\dfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_0+\dfrac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\right]a_1=4\pi G\rho_0\,a_1$.
steps.explain: Linearise around $a_0$: $\rho a$ scales like $a^{-2}$, so its derivative brings a factor $-2$. Collect the terms proportional to $a_1$ and use the static condition.

steps.reveal: $a_1\propto e^{\pm\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_0}\,t}$: the growing mode wins. A slight expansion lowers the density, gravity weakens, $\Lambda$ wins and expansion accelerates (and vice versa): the static universe is unstable, which is why Einstein’s model could not describe the real Universe even before Hubble.
steps.explain: A positive coefficient means exponential growth or decay: an unstable equilibrium, like a ball on a hilltop.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.4: Free particles slow down as $1/a$; decoupled relics
enc.goal: (a) For a free particle in the Robertson–Walker metric moving in $\chi$ only, show from the extremum of $\int ds$ that $a^2d\chi/d\tau$ is a constant, so the peculiar velocity decays as $a^{-1}$. (b) Particles in equilibrium while relativistic decouple and later become non-relativistic. Show that (11.7) keeps holding with $T\propto a^{-1}$. Is that $T$ a true temperature? Does (11.8) still hold? How do you find their density?

steps.reveal: The Lagrangian $\sqrt{c^2\dot t^2-a^2\dot\chi^2}$ does not contain $\chi$, so $a^2\,d\chi/d\tau$ is conserved. Peculiar velocity $v=a\,d\chi/dt$ with $\gamma v=a\,d\chi/d\tau\propto1/a$: momentum $\propto a^{-1}$, and for slow particles $v\propto a^{-1}$.
steps.explain: The action does not depend on $\chi$ (homogeneity), so the conjugate momentum is conserved: $a^2d\chi/d\tau$. Physical momentum is $a\,d\chi/d\tau\propto1/a$: it redshifts like a photon's.

steps.reveal: Every particle’s momentum scales as $p\propto1/a$ and the number in a comoving volume is fixed. The occupation number $f(p)=1/(e^{pc/\kappa_BT}\pm1)$ is conserved along the flow, so it keeps its form with $T\propto1/a$: (11.7) still holds.
steps.explain: All momenta shrink by the same factor, so the shape of the distribution is preserved; only the parameter $T$ scales as $1/a$.

steps.reveal: It is only a parameter of the momentum distribution: the particles no longer interact, and once non-relativistic their energy is not $pc$, so the distribution is not Bose–Einstein or Fermi–Dirac in energy.
steps.explain: A temperature describes equilibrium in energy. Once the particles are non-relativistic and no longer interact, the distribution is not an equilibrium distribution in energy any more.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.5: Coordinate distance against redshift for $k=-1$
enc.goal: For $k=-1$ and $\Lambda=0$, derive the relation between coordinate distance $r$ and redshift $z$, and show it is the same as (14.32) for $k=+1$.

steps.reveal: $\sinh^{-1}r$; right side: $\displaystyle\int_0^z\frac{c\,dz}{a_0H_0\sqrt{\Omega_{M,0}(1+z)^3+(1-\Omega_{M,0})(1+z)^2}}$.
steps.explain: A light ray: $ds=0$ radially, so $\frac{a\,dr}{\sqrt{1+r^2}}=c\,dt$ for $k=-1$. Change variable from $t$ to $z$ with $dt=-\frac{dz}{(1+z)H}$.

steps.reveal: With $\Omega\equiv\Omega_{M,0}<1$ the integral is elementary (substitute $1+z=1/x$); taking $\sinh$ of the result gives (Mattig) $r=\dfrac{c}{a_0H_0}\dfrac{2\left[\Omega z+(2-\Omega)\left(1-\sqrt{1+\Omega z}\right)\right]}{\Omega^2(1+z)}$.
steps.explain: The $z$ integral is elementary with the substitution suggested; then take $\sinh$ of both sides to isolate $r$.

steps.reveal: This is the same expression as for $k=+1$ (where $\sin^{-1}$ and $\sin$ appear instead): the curvature sign only enters through $a_0H_0$. Hence one formula holds for all $\Omega$, and it reduces to $r\,a_0H_0/c=2\left(1-1/\sqrt{1+z}\right)$ for $\Omega=1$.
steps.explain: The $k=+1$ calculation has $\sin$ where this one has $\sinh$; with the corresponding relation between $a_0H_0$ and $\Omega$ both give the same formula.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.6: Galaxy counts per redshift interval
enc.goal: If there are $n$ galaxies per unit comoving volume, find the number within solid angle $d\Omega$ with redshifts in $[z,z+dz]$.

steps.reveal: $dN=n\dfrac{a_0^3r^2}{\sqrt{1-kr^2}}\dfrac{dr}{dz}dz\,d\Omega$.
steps.explain: Number = density × comoving volume of the shell between $z$ and $z+dz$; the volume element follows from the Robertson–Walker metric.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{dr}{\sqrt{1-kr^2}}=\dfrac{c\,dz}{a_0H(z)}$, so $dN=n\dfrac{c\,a_0^2r^2(z)}{H(z)}dz\,d\Omega$.
steps.explain: The light-ray relation links $dr$ to $dz$ via the Hubble rate at that redshift.

steps.reveal: $a_0r=\dfrac{2c}{H_0}\left(1-\dfrac1{\sqrt{1+z}}\right)$, $H=H_0(1+z)^{3/2}$: $dN=n\left(\dfrac c{H_0}\right)^3\dfrac{4\left(1-(1+z)^{-1/2}\right)^2}{(1+z)^{3/2}}dz\,d\Omega$. The counts grow as $z^2$ at small $z$ and then turn over: number counts test the geometry (if galaxies did not evolve).
steps.explain: Insert the matter-only expressions. At small $z$ the shell volume grows as $z^2$; at large $z$ the expansion history makes it shrink again.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.7: Standard candles: luminosity distance for three cosmologies
enc.goal: Using (14.51), numerically evaluate and plot the apparent luminosity of standard candles against $z$ for (i) $\Omega_M=1,\Omega_\Lambda=0$, (ii) $\Omega_M=0,\Omega_\Lambda=1$, (iii) $\Omega_M=0.3,\Omega_\Lambda=0.7$.

steps.prompt: All three are flat, so $S(x)\to x$.
steps.reveal: $d_L=(1+z)\dfrac c{H_0}\displaystyle\int_0^z\frac{dz'}{E(z')}$.
steps.explain: $\kappa=1-\Omega_M-\Omega_\Lambda=0$ for all three, and $S(x)/\sqrt{|\kappa|}\to x$ as $\kappa\to0$.
Numerical integration of $1/E(z)$; the closed forms check the program.

steps.reveal: $l\propto d_L^{-2}$: at a given $z$ candles are faintest in the $\Lambda$-dominated model. At $z=0.5$, model (iii) is $(0.661/0.551)^2\approx1.44$ times fainter than EdS, i.e. 0.4 mag: what the 1998 supernova observations found (accelerating Universe).
steps.explain: Brightness $\propto1/d_L^2$. A larger $d_L$ at the same $z$ means fainter; the $\Lambda$ model has the largest distances because expansion was slower in the past. $2.5\log_{10}(1.44)\approx0.4$ mag.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.8: Legendre coefficients of a Gaussian correlation function
enc.goal: For $C(\theta)=e^{-(\theta/\theta_0)^2}$ expanded as $C=\sum\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}C_lP_l(\cos\theta)$ (14.53), show $C_l=2\pi\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{+1}C(\theta)P_l(\cos\theta)\,d(\cos\theta)$. Write a code for the $C_l$, run it for a few $\theta_0$ and find the $l$ where $C_l$ is maximum.
given: Note: Our text copy asks for the maximum of $C_l$; for a Gaussian that is $l=0$, so the useful statement is the peak of $l(l+1)C_l$, as plotted for the CMB.

steps.reveal: Multiply (14.53) by $P_{l'}(\cos\theta)$ and integrate over $x=\cos\theta$: $\int CP_{l'}dx=\frac{2l'+1}{4\pi}C_{l'}\frac2{2l'+1}=\frac{C_{l'}}{2\pi}$, so $C_l=2\pi\int_{-1}^1CP_l\,dx$.
steps.explain: Orthogonality of Legendre polynomials works exactly like orthogonality of $\cos(nx)$ in Fourier series: multiply both sides by $P_{l'}$, integrate, and only the $l=l'$ term survives.

steps.reveal: Integrate $2\pi\int_0^\pi e^{-(\theta/\theta_0)^2}P_l(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta$ (only $\theta\lesssim5\theta_0$ matters), with $P_l$ from the recurrence $(l+1)P_{l+1}=(2l+1)xP_l-lP_{l-1}$, for $l=0\ldots10/\theta_0$.
steps.explain: Use $x=\cos\theta$ and the recurrence to generate $P_l$ stably; the Gaussian is negligible beyond a few $\theta_0$.

steps.reveal: For small $\theta_0$, $C_l\approx\pi\theta_0^2e^{-l(l+1)\theta_0^2/4}$: $C_l$ itself is largest at $l=0$ and decreases. The quantity plotted for the CMB, $l(l+1)C_l$, peaks at $l\approx2/\theta_0$: computed $l=114$, $22$, $11$ for $\theta_0=1^\circ,5^\circ,10^\circ$ (prediction $115$, $22.9$, $11.5$).
steps.explain: For a narrow Gaussian $P_l(\cos\theta)\approx J_0(l\theta)$ and the integral is again Gaussian in $l$. Multiplying by $l(l+1)$ shifts the peak to $l\sim2/\theta_0$.

steps.reveal: Structure of angular size $\theta$ shows up at $l\sim\pi/\theta$: the first acoustic peak at $l\approx200$ corresponds to $\approx1^\circ$, the sound horizon at recombination seen in a flat Universe.
steps.explain: An angular scale $\theta$ corresponds to multipole $l\sim\pi/\theta$, like wavelength and wave number. The CMB peak at $l\approx200$ is the $1^\circ$ sound horizon.
